rental-deposit-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The advert shows a bright two-bedroom flat in a good street, at a rent noticeably below everything else you have seen that week. You message, and the owner answers quickly and pleasantly. They explain that they have moved overseas for work, so viewings are difficult, but the place is yours if you can commit. When you have spent weeks losing flats to faster applicants, a landlord who wants you feels like a break. The photographs are real, the address exists, and the tenancy agreement they email has a name and signature on it.

The listing is a copy. Its pictures and description were lifted from a genuine sale or letting advert, sometimes for a property that was let months ago. The person writing to you has no connection to the building. They want a holding deposit and the first month's rent sent by bank transfer, e-transfer or a payment app, and often an "application form" with your passport, payslips and bank details as well. Once the money lands it is moved on within hours. The keys that were promised by courier never arrive, and the same advert is run again for the next applicant.

The rule is to pay nothing until you, or someone you trust, have stood inside the property with a person who has shown they are entitled to let it. A drive past the outside does not count, and neither does a set of photographs or a video clip. An owner can prove ownership, an agent can be reached through the agency's published number, and both can open the front door. Anyone who cannot arrange that, yet has a reason why the deposit must come first, is selling a flat that is not theirs.

howItWorks.title: A copied listing goes up
howItWorks.detail: Photos and wording from a real advert are reposted on a classifieds site or social marketplace with a new contact number and a rent set well under the local rate.

howItWorks.title: The absent owner's story
howItWorks.detail: Replies come from someone abroad on a work posting, a mission trip or caring for a relative. They are friendly, ask about your job and pets, and say they want a careful tenant.

howItWorks.title: Paperwork that looks official
howItWorks.detail: An application form requests your ID, employer and bank details. A lease follows, sometimes bearing the real owner's name taken from public property records, to make payment feel like the last formality.

howItWorks.title: Money to hold it
howItWorks.detail: You are told two other applicants are ready, so the deposit and first month must be sent today to an individual's account. The keys will be couriered once it clears.

howItWorks.title: Delays, then silence
howItWorks.detail: A courier fee or an extra month's security is requested next. When payments stop, the number goes dead and the advert reappears under another name with the same pictures.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Priya had accepted a nursing post in a city four hours away and needed somewhere to live within a month. On a social marketplace she found a one-bedroom flat near the hospital for 750, when similar places were over 1,000. The owner, "Daniel", wrote that he was on an engineering contract overseas. He sent a lease and asked for 750 rent plus a 750 deposit by bank transfer, after which a courier would bring the keys. He added that a couple were also interested and he would prefer a nurse.

The account name on the payment request was not Daniel's, which made Priya pause. She ran the living room photo through an image search and found the flat on an estate agent's website, marked as sold the previous spring. She rang the agency, who confirmed it was not available to rent and that they had never heard of Daniel. Priya sent nothing, reported the advert to the marketplace, and booked a short stay so she could view places in person. This account is fictional, written to show how the pieces usually fit together.

variations.name: The lockbox self-viewing
variations.detail: The scammer books a self-guided tour with a real letting company, obtains the door code, and passes it to you. Seeing inside convinces you, but the deposit goes to them.

variations.name: The short-let sublet
variations.detail: Someone rents a holiday apartment for a few nights, shows several hopeful tenants round as its "landlord", takes a deposit from each, and checks out before move-in day.

variations.name: The paid credit check
variations.detail: Before any viewing you must buy a credit report through a link the "landlord" supplies. The site harvests card details and identity documents, and no viewing date is ever offered.

variations.name: Student and newcomer targeting
variations.detail: Adverts appear in university housing groups just before term, aimed at people arriving from abroad who cannot view. Payment is requested by international transfer to secure the room in advance.

realVsFake.real: A landlord or agent arranges a viewing inside the property, in person or through someone local who holds the keys.
realVsFake.fake: The owner is abroad with nobody nearby to let you in, and suggests you look at the building from the pavement.

realVsFake.real: A letting agency takes payment into a business account in the agency's name and issues a receipt.
realVsFake.fake: The deposit is to go to a personal account, a payment app handle or a name that differs from the person you have been emailing.

realVsFake.real: A genuine owner can show proof of ownership that matches the public property record, and the name agrees with their identification.
realVsFake.fake: The "landlord" sends a passport photo as proof, which may itself be stolen from an earlier applicant.

realVsFake.real: Keys are handed over at the property when the agreement is signed, usually with an inventory check.
realVsFake.fake: Keys will supposedly arrive by courier after payment clears, and the courier then needs a fee of its own.

verify: Run two of the listing photos through Google Lens or TinEye. Matches on a sale advert, a hotel site or a listing in another city mean the pictures were copied.
Search the full address in quotation marks. If an agency also advertises it, ring that agency on the number from its own website and ask who is letting it.
Look up who owns the address in the public property record, such as the land registry or county assessor, and compare that name with the landlord's.
Ask for a live video walkthrough today that starts at the street door and shows them unlocking it. A recorded clip or a refusal tells you enough.
Compare the name on the bank or e-transfer details with the name on the lease. If they differ, or the account is overseas, do not send the deposit.

sources.title: Check if something might be a scam

romance-mule-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: By the time the request comes, you have been talking for weeks. They have said good morning every day, remembered your sister's name and talked about a future together. Then a practical problem appears. A client's payment cannot reach their account abroad, or their bank has frozen their funds during a contract overseas. They ask whether the money could arrive in your account instead, just this once, for you to pass on. It costs you nothing. You are being asked for a favour, and people help the ones they love.

The partner is after your bank account more than your savings. The money that arrives was taken from other victims, often people caught in the same romance script or a business tricked into paying a false invoice. Passing it through an ordinary account in a real person's name hides where it came from. You are told to forward it by wire, to buy cryptocurrency with it, or to withdraw cash and deposit it elsewhere. When the first victim's bank traces the payment, the trail stops at you: your name, your account, your signature on the transfer.

Your bank account exists to hold your own money and nobody else's. No honest partner, employer or business needs a private individual's account to receive funds and send them on, and no explanation changes that. If someone you have never met in person asks you to accept a payment and forward it, decline, however small the sum and however reasonable the story. If money has already arrived, leave it where it is and tell your bank. Sending it onward, even to get rid of it, is the step that completes the laundering.

howItWorks.title: Courtship comes first
howItWorks.detail: A match on a dating app or social network becomes a daily conversation. The person is attentive, works abroad on a rig, a ship or a posting, and cannot meet yet.

howItWorks.title: A banking problem appears
howItWorks.detail: Their account is frozen, their employer pays only into domestic banks, or a customer needs somewhere local to send funds. They ask for your account number and the name on it.

howItWorks.title: Strangers' money lands
howItWorks.detail: Deposits arrive from people or companies you do not know, with odd payment references. Each one is another victim's loss, sent to you because they were given your details.

howItWorks.title: Forward it quickly
howItWorks.detail: You receive precise instructions: wire it to a named account, convert it at a crypto cash machine, or buy gift cards. Speed matters to them, since the sending bank may recall it.

howItWorks.title: The account holder answers
howItWorks.detail: Fraud reports lead investigators to your account. The bank restricts or closes it, may ask you to repay sums you forwarded, and the partner stops replying or finds a new story.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Teresa, a widowed school cook, had been messaging "Mark" for two months. He said he was a marine engineer finishing a contract at sea. One evening he explained that a supplier needed to refund him 2,400 but could only pay a local account. He asked her to receive it and send it on to his business partner. The money arrived the next morning from a woman Teresa had never heard of, with the reference "loan for M". Mark sent the partner's account details at once and asked her to transfer it before lunch.

The reference bothered her. A supplier's refund would not be labelled as a loan from a private person. Instead of forwarding the money, Teresa rang her bank on the number printed on her card and described the whole arrangement. The bank told her the payment had already been reported by the sender as fraud, held the funds and returned them. Teresa stopped replying to Mark and filed a report with the national fraud reporting service. She is a fictional character, and the outcome here is tidier than many real cases turn out to be.

variations.name: Open an account for me
variations.detail: The partner asks you to open a new bank or payment app account in your name and hand over the login, so the transfers happen without you seeing them.

variations.name: Parcels instead of payments
variations.detail: Phones, laptops or designer goods bought with stolen cards are delivered to your address. You are asked to repackage them and post them abroad using labels the partner emails.

variations.name: The cheque to deposit
variations.detail: A cheque arrives by post for you to pay in and send most of the value onward. It is later returned as forged, and your bank takes the full amount back.

variations.name: Victim first, mule second
variations.detail: Someone who has already sent their own savings is told the only way to recover them is to help move "company funds", turning a defrauded person into a courier.

realVsFake.real: A functioning business takes customer payments into a business account held in its own name.
realVsFake.fake: The partner's "company" needs your personal current account because theirs is frozen, under audit or in the wrong country.

realVsFake.real: A partner who owes you money pays you back, and the sum stays with you.
realVsFake.fake: Money arrives from a stranger, and you are given a third person's account to forward it to the same day.

realVsFake.real: Someone genuinely working overseas still has a bank, an employer and colleagues who can sort out a payment problem.
realVsFake.fake: You are the only person on earth who can help, and the arrangement must stay between the two of you.

realVsFake.real: A bank holds the named account holder responsible for the payments that pass through the account.
realVsFake.fake: They call it only a favour, offer you a share to keep, and supply a cover story to tell the cashier.

verify: Open your banking app and read the names and references on recent incoming payments. Senders you have never dealt with are the clearest sign of other victims.
Leave any received money untouched and call the fraud line on the back of your bank card. Say you think your account has been used to pass on funds.
Put their profile pictures through a reverse image search. Photos of soldiers, doctors and engineers are routinely lifted from real people's social media pages.
Scroll back and list every request involving money, with dates and amounts. Seeing receive-and-forward written down makes the pattern plain, and gives the bank something to work from.
Tell one friend or relative exactly what you were asked to do with the money. Secrecy is part of the script, and an outside view breaks it.

steam-phishing-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: A message pops up from someone on your friends list, often a person you have played with for years. They ask you to vote for their team in a tournament, offer a skin they no longer want, or confess that they "accidentally reported" your account and that an admin needs to hear from you before a ban goes through. The link opens what appears to be the normal Steam or Discord sign-in. It works because the sender's own account was taken the same way an hour earlier, so the request arrives with a trusted name and avatar attached.

The target is the account and what it holds. The fake page relays your username, password and Steam Guard code to the real site as you type, signing the criminal in beside you. Inventory items with resale value, such as Counter-Strike skins, are traded out to accounts they control. Wallet balance is spent on gifts or market items. On Discord, a scanned QR code or stolen login token hands over the session without any password. Your account then messages everyone you know with the same link.

Treat every sign-in prompt that arrives through a message as fake. Valve staff do not contact players on Discord or in Steam chat about reports, and nobody at either company needs your password, a Steam Guard code or a QR scan to clear your name. If you think something is wrong with your account, close the message and open the Steam client or the Discord app yourself. A real restriction will be shown there. And where a friend is the sender, ask them by voice or text whether they sent it.

howItWorks.title: A hijacked friend messages
howItWorks.detail: The link comes from an account you know, already compromised. The wording is casual: a tournament vote, a free knife skin, a Nitro gift, or an apology for reporting you by mistake.

howItWorks.title: The counterfeit sign-in window
howItWorks.detail: The site offers "Sign in through Steam". The pop-up that appears is drawn inside the web page, complete with a fake address bar showing the genuine Steam address.

howItWorks.title: Credentials relayed live
howItWorks.detail: Whatever you type is passed to the real login within seconds. When Steam asks for a Steam Guard code, the fake page asks you too, and forwards your answer.

howItWorks.title: Quiet changes behind you
howItWorks.detail: Once inside, the intruder may register a Web API key on your account, which lets their software watch and cancel your trade offers even after a password change.

howItWorks.title: Inventory out, links onward
howItWorks.detail: Valuable items are moved to holding accounts, sometimes by swapping a real trade for an identical-looking one from an impostor. Your account then sends the bait to your friends list.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Kofi, a college student, got a Discord message from a friend he played Counter-Strike with most weekends. The friend asked him to vote for his team in a small online tournament and pasted a link. The page had team logos and a "Sign in through Steam" button. A sign-in window opened, showing the usual Steam address at the top. Kofi typed his username and password, then the code from his authenticator. The window closed and the vote page said "thank you". He thought nothing more of it and went back to his game.

Ten minutes later his phone showed a Steam confirmation request for a trade he had not started, sending three skins to an unfamiliar profile. He declined it. Then he changed his password from the Steam client, deauthorised all other devices in the Steam Guard settings, and found a Web API key registered that he had never created, which he revoked. He phoned his friend, who had lost his own account that afternoon. Kofi kept his inventory. He is an invented example, though the fake vote page and the planted API key are both common in real takeovers.

variations.name: The accidental report
variations.detail: A stranger or friend claims they reported you for fraud by mistake and sends you to a "Steam admin" on Discord, who demands a login, gift cards or your items for "safekeeping".

variations.name: Discord QR code login
variations.detail: A bot or user asks you to scan a QR code to "verify" or claim Nitro. Scanning it with the Discord mobile app signs their computer in to your account.

variations.name: Try my game download
variations.detail: Someone asks you to test a game they are building and sends a file. It is malware that copies saved passwords and login tokens from your browser and Discord client.

variations.name: The middleman trade
variations.detail: During a high-value swap, the other trader insists on a "trusted middleman" or a price-check bot. The go-between is their second account, and items sent to it are gone.

realVsFake.real: Steam shows bans and restrictions on the account itself, visible when you sign in through the client or the official support site.
realVsFake.fake: A Discord user calling themselves a Steam admin says a ban is pending and only they can cancel it.

realVsFake.real: A genuine Steam sign-in pop-up is a separate browser window that you can drag anywhere on your desktop.
realVsFake.fake: The counterfeit window is an image inside the page. It cannot be dragged past the edge of the tab that contains it.

realVsFake.real: Steam Guard codes are entered only into Steam itself when you are the one starting a sign-in.
realVsFake.fake: A voting, giveaway or appeal site asks for the current code, or a "support agent" asks you to read it out in chat.

realVsFake.real: Discord's own notices arrive as system messages carrying an official badge, and they never ask for your password or token.
realVsFake.fake: An ordinary user account with a staff-style name and logo messages you about a violation and links to a "verification" page.

verify: Click and drag the sign-in pop-up towards the edge of your screen. If it stops at the border of the browser tab, it is a fake drawn on the page.
Open the Steam client yourself and check your account through Help, then Steam Support. A genuine ban or lock shows on the account, not in a chat message.
Phone or text the friend who sent the link, using a channel other than Steam or Discord, and ask whether they wrote it.
If you typed anything in, change your Steam password from the client, choose "Deauthorize all other devices" under Steam Guard, and revoke any Web API key you did not create.
In Discord, open User Settings, then Devices, and log out every session you do not recognise. Changing your password also invalidates a stolen login token.

auto-warranty-call-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The phone rings from a number with your own area code. A recorded voice says they have been trying to reach you about your vehicle's factory cover, that this is the final courtesy call before your file is closed, and that you should press 1 to speak to a specialist. Most people own a car and few could say from memory when its warranty runs out. The recording names no manufacturer and no model, which lets it fit almost anyone who answers. The suggestion that something is about to lapse does the rest.

Pressing 1 connects you to a salesperson working from a script. They ask for the make, model and mileage, quote a price for a "protection plan", and push for a down payment by card before the call ends. Some of these operations sell nothing at all and simply collect card numbers. Others sell a third-party service contract with so many exclusions that claims are refused, billed monthly and hard to cancel. Along the way they may ask for your vehicle identification number, driving licence and date of birth, which have a resale value of their own.

A manufacturer's warranty does not need renewing by phone. It runs for a set period or mileage from the day the car was first sold, and then it ends. Anything offered afterwards is a separate service contract, which you are free to buy or ignore and should only ever buy after reading it. So the working rule is simple: never buy vehicle cover on a call you did not make. In the United States, a recorded sales call to someone who has not agreed to it in writing already breaks telemarketing rules, whatever the product.

howItWorks.title: Mass dialling, local numbers
howItWorks.detail: Software places calls in bulk and displays a caller ID copied to resemble a nearby number. The same recording plays to drivers, non-drivers and people who sold their car long ago.

howItWorks.title: The final-notice recording
howItWorks.detail: A calm voice refers to earlier attempts to reach you and a file about to close. It offers two keys: one for a specialist, another supposedly to be removed from the list.

howItWorks.title: Fishing for vehicle details
howItWorks.detail: The live agent opens by asking what you drive and how many miles it has done. Your answers let them sound informed and repeat the details back as if on record.

howItWorks.title: A quote with a deadline
howItWorks.detail: A plan is priced on the spot, with a discount that lasts only for this call. Requests to see the contract first are met with a promise to post it after enrolment.

howItWorks.title: Card taken, charges recur
howItWorks.detail: You read out a card number for the down payment. Monthly debits follow under an unfamiliar company name, and the cancellation line rings out or demands a fee.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Darnell drove a seven-year-old pickup he had bought used. A recorded call told him his warranty was expiring and he pressed 1, half curious. A fast-talking agent asked for the make, mileage and his postcode, then said he qualified for "full bumper-to-bumper protection" at 2,900, with 195 down today and the rest monthly. When Darnell asked which company would pay a repair claim, the agent said the details were in the welcome pack. When he asked to read the contract before paying, the agent said the price could not be held.

That refusal decided it. Darnell knew the truck's original warranty had ended years before he bought it, so there was nothing to expire. He hung up without giving a card number. He found the manufacturer's owner site, entered the vehicle identification number from the door frame, and confirmed no factory cover remained. Then he blocked the number and filed a short report with the consumer protection agency. The calls kept coming for a while, from different numbers, and he let them ring. Darnell's story is illustrative and does not describe a real person.

variations.name: The final-notice postcard
variations.detail: A card or letter headed "Motor Vehicle Notification" arrives, styled like official mail with a response deadline and a freephone number that leads to the same sales room.

variations.name: The dealership impersonator
variations.detail: The caller names your actual make and model, drawn from sold marketing data or public records, and says they are ringing from the dealer's service department about lapsed cover.

variations.name: The expiry text message
variations.detail: A text says your vehicle's coverage has ended and gives a number to call for reactivation. It reaches people whose phones already silence calls from unknown numbers.

variations.name: The cancellation refund call
variations.detail: Weeks after you pay, someone rings offering to cancel the plan and refund you, then asks for bank details or a fee. It is a second pass at the same customer.

realVsFake.real: A factory warranty is set by the car's age and mileage and is written in the booklet that came with the vehicle.
realVsFake.fake: The recording says cover is about to end without naming your car, its maker or any policy number.

realVsFake.real: A reputable service contract seller gives you the full terms to read first and names the administrator that pays claims.
realVsFake.fake: The agent wants a card number for a down payment now and says the paperwork will be posted afterwards.

realVsFake.real: Your dealer or manufacturer already holds your vehicle's records and can quote them to you.
realVsFake.fake: The specialist's opening question is what make and model you drive, because the call was placed blind.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate company gives a business name and address you can look up, and will call back at a time you choose.
realVsFake.fake: The caller uses a vague title such as "vehicle services department" and hangs up when asked for a registered company name.

verify: Hang up without pressing a key, including the one offered for removal from the list. Any key press tells the dialler a person answered.
Find the warranty booklet in the glovebox and check the stated period and mileage limit against your odometer and the date the car was first registered.
Ring your dealer's service desk on the number from a past invoice and give the vehicle identification number. They can say in a minute whether any cover is active.
If an agent gave a company name, search it together with the word "complaints" and look it up on the BBB Scam Tracker before calling anyone back.
If you read out a card number, open your card app, check for pending charges, and call the issuer to block that merchant and replace the card.

fake-e-transfer-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: An email or text says an INTERAC e-Transfer is waiting: 250.00 from a name you half recognise, a tax rebate, or a refund from a phone company. There is a yellow logo, a reference number and a button marked "Deposit your money". People in Canada receive genuine notices like this all the time, from friends splitting a bill or buyers paying for something sold online, so the format raises no suspicion. Pressing the button brings up a list of bank logos, exactly as the real service does. You pick yours and a familiar sign-in page appears.

No transfer exists. The bank selection screen and the sign-in page are copies hosted on the criminal's own site. Whatever you enter, card number, password, answers to your verification questions, and any code texted to your phone, is captured and used straight away on your real online banking. Once signed in as you, the criminal sends e-Transfers out to accounts held by accomplices, adds new payees, and may change the contact details on file so that alerts stop reaching you. The promised 250 was the bait for access to everything else.

Turn on Autodeposit in your banking app and the problem largely disappears. With it registered, money sent to your email address or mobile number goes directly into your account, and the notice you get simply reports that it has arrived. Nothing needs claiming. From then on, any message telling you to deposit a transfer sent to that address can be treated as fake. Until it is set up, treat an unexpected notice as unconfirmed: contact the sender yourself, and do not sign in to your bank through the message.

howItWorks.title: A notice that looks routine
howItWorks.detail: The message copies Interac's layout and names a sender such as a government agency, a utility or a common first name, with an amount small enough to seem plausible.

howItWorks.title: Pick your bank
howItWorks.detail: The deposit button opens an imitation of the screen where you select your financial institution. Each logo links to a cloned sign-in page for that particular bank or credit union.

howItWorks.title: Login details collected
howItWorks.detail: You enter your card number and password. The page often reports an error and asks again, or moves on to your security questions, mother's maiden name and date of birth.

howItWorks.title: The one-time code request
howItWorks.detail: While you wait, the criminal signs in at the real bank, which texts you a verification code. The fake page asks for it, and you unknowingly approve their session.

howItWorks.title: Money leaves by e-Transfer
howItWorks.detail: Using your own account, they send transfers to recipients who cash out quickly. You are shown a "deposit successful" screen or redirected to the genuine bank homepage to delay suspicion.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Nadia runs a small alterations business from home in Winnipeg and is paid by e-Transfer several times a week. One afternoon a text announced a transfer of 180.00 from "S. Tremblay". She had a customer by that surname, so she tapped the link. A page of bank logos appeared, she chose her credit union, and a sign-in screen loaded. She entered her member number and password. The page then asked for her three security questions and their answers, all on one screen, before she could "complete the deposit".

Her credit union had only ever asked one question at a time. Nadia looked at the address bar and saw a string of words ending in a domain she did not know. She closed the tab, opened the credit union's app, and changed her password there. Then she called the number on her debit card. The agent found a new login attempt from another province, blocked it, and helped her switch on Autodeposit for her business email. Nadia is a fictional example, built from the way these fake deposit pages typically behave.

variations.name: Government rebate by text
variations.detail: A text claims a tax refund or benefit payment has been sent by e-Transfer and must be accepted. The Canada Revenue Agency does not pay refunds by e-Transfer or text links.

variations.name: The request disguised as payment
variations.detail: A buyer of something you are selling sends a genuine Request Money notice instead of a payment. Approving it sends your funds to them, when you expected to receive theirs.

variations.name: The pending transfer fee
variations.detail: A forged notice says the buyer's payment is on hold because your account has a receiving limit, and that you must send money first to "expand" it and release the funds.

variations.name: The fake Autodeposit confirmation
variations.detail: A seller receives an email styled as an automatic deposit notice and hands over the goods. No money arrived, which a glance at the account balance would have shown.

realVsFake.real: With Autodeposit registered, an Interac e-Transfer lands in your account by itself and the notice only reports that it arrived.
realVsFake.fake: The message insists funds are waiting to be claimed through its button, although Autodeposit is switched on for that address.

realVsFake.real: A genuine manual deposit asks only for the answer to the question the sender set, after you sign in at your own bank.
realVsFake.fake: The cloned page collects your card number, password and every personal verification question, then asks for a texted code.

realVsFake.real: An unclaimed Interac e-Transfer normally stays available for around thirty days before returning to the sender.
realVsFake.fake: The notice warns the deposit will be cancelled within hours unless you sign in straight away.

realVsFake.real: Depositing an Interac e-Transfer never requires you to send money first or to pay to raise a limit.
realVsFake.fake: A "pending" transfer comes with instructions to send a matching amount or a release fee before the funds can be freed.

verify: Open your banking app, find the Interac e-Transfer settings and check whether Autodeposit is registered for the address the notice was sent to.
Call or text the named sender on a number you already hold and ask whether they sent that amount today. For an agency or utility, assume not.
Press and hold the deposit button, or hover over it on a computer, to preview where it leads. An address unrelated to Interac or your bank is a forgery.
If you already signed in through the link, change your online banking password inside the official app now, then ring the number on your bank card.
Check your recent transactions, e-Transfer history and payee list for anything you did not create, and ask the bank to cancel any transfer still pending.

puppy-sale-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: A litter of French bulldog or dachshund puppies sits in a basket in the photographs, priced several hundred below every other breeder you have found. The seller replies within minutes and seems to care: they ask whether you have a garden, other pets, children. They send more photos and a short clip of the puppy you chose. People looking for a dog have usually already decided they want one, and the questions make the seller sound responsible. Being asked for a small deposit to reserve her feels like the normal next step.

There is no puppy. The pictures were taken from a real breeder's page or an old advert. The deposit is only the opening charge. After it is paid, an email arrives from a "pet transport company" with a tracking page, followed by a demand for a refundable temperature-controlled crate, then travel insurance, then a vaccination or quarantine certificate. Each fee is said to be the last and promised back on delivery. Payments are requested by e-transfer, payment app, wire or gift card, because those are difficult to reverse once the buyer realises nothing is coming.

Send no money until you have seen the animal alive and responding to you, either in person where it was bred or on a live video call that you direct. Ask the seller to say your name, pick the puppy up and turn it round, and show its mother. A breeder with a real litter can do this in five minutes and will usually be glad to. A seller who offers only more photographs, a pre-recorded clip or a reason the camera is broken has answered the question for you.

howItWorks.title: An appealing litter advertised
howItWorks.detail: Stolen photos of a popular breed are posted on a classifieds site, a social media group or a purpose-built "family breeder" website, at a price that undercuts genuine sellers.

howItWorks.title: A caring seller responds
howItWorks.detail: Replies are warm and quick. The seller asks about your home, explains they live far away, and offers delivery by a pet courier in place of a visit.

howItWorks.title: The reservation deposit
howItWorks.detail: The seller mentions another interested family, so a deposit by e-transfer or payment app will hold her. A contract or "health guarantee" document arrives to make it feel formal.

howItWorks.title: The courier takes over
howItWorks.detail: A shipping company you did not choose emails a tracking number. Its website shows the puppy "in transit", then held at an airport pending a special crate or insurance payment.

howItWorks.title: Fees until you stop
howItWorks.detail: Each payment produces a new obstacle: a vet certificate, a customs charge, a permit. Refusal brings threats that you will be reported for abandoning the animal.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Owen and his daughter had wanted a miniature dachshund for a year. He found a breeder's page on social media with a litter at 600 each, about half the usual price. The seller, "Claire", said she was moving house and needed the puppies settled quickly. Owen sent a 150 deposit by bank transfer. The next day a courier firm emailed to say the puppy was booked for delivery but airline rules required a climate-controlled crate, costing 380, refundable when the driver handed her over.

Owen had not chosen a courier, and the firm's email came from a free webmail address. He asked Claire for a video call with the puppy before paying anything more. She said her camera was broken and sent the same clip as before. He searched one of the photos and found it on a breeder's site in another country, posted two years earlier. He stopped paying, told his bank about the transfer, and reported the page. This example is invented, but the crate fee after the deposit is the usual sequence.

variations.name: Free to a good home
variations.detail: The animal is offered at no charge because the owner is ill, bereaved or relocating. You only cover transport, and the transport is where every fee is collected.

variations.name: The cloned breeder
variations.detail: A real kennel's name, registration prefix and photographs are copied onto a new website or profile with different contact details. Checks on the kennel's name come back clean.

variations.name: Kittens, parrots and exotics
variations.detail: The same script sells Maine Coon and Sphynx kittens, parrots, and reptiles. Rarer animals justify higher transport and permit fees, and buyers expect them to come from far away.

variations.name: The sponsored social page
variations.detail: A paid advert leads to a polished page with reviews and a countdown on the "last available" puppy. Comments are switched off or filled with praise from newly created profiles.

realVsFake.real: A responsible breeder invites you to visit, shows the litter with its mother, and often questions you closely in return.
realVsFake.fake: The seller always lives hours away, has a reason visits cannot happen, and steers you towards delivery to your door.

realVsFake.real: A licensed pet transporter quotes the whole cost before the journey and is booked by you or the breeder in advance.
realVsFake.fake: A courier nobody mentioned writes mid-journey demanding a refundable crate or insurance payment before the puppy can continue.

realVsFake.real: A genuine breeder names the veterinary practice that examined the litter and hands over vaccination records stamped by that practice.
realVsFake.fake: Health papers come as a photographed certificate with no clinic phone number, or with one that only the seller answers.

realVsFake.real: Breeders of pedigree dogs can give registration details for the parents that the kennel club can check.
realVsFake.fake: The advert says "registered, papers included" but no registration number is supplied, however often you ask.

verify: Request a video call right now and have the seller say your name while holding the puppy. A clip sent afterwards is not a substitute.
Reverse search the puppy photos with Google Lens. Finding the same litter on another breeder's site, or in an advert from a previous season, ends the matter.
Paste the seller's phone number, email address and website name into a search engine with the word "scam". Earlier buyers often post warnings on pet scam listing sites.
Ask for the parents' kennel club registration numbers and check them with the club yourself. For a UK puppy, ask for the microchip number, which must exist before sale.
Check the age of the breeder's website with a free WHOIS lookup. A kennel claiming decades of experience on a site created last month is lying.

two-factor-code-text-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: A six-digit code lands on your phone from the short number your bank, email provider or WhatsApp always uses. You did not ask for it. Seconds later someone gets in touch: a caller from "account security", a marketplace buyer, or a friend whose message says the code was sent to you by mistake. The text is real, which is what makes the request feel safe. It sits in the same thread as every code you have ever received, and the person contacting you predicted its arrival, so their story seems to check out.

The code exists because the criminal is already standing at your front door. They have typed your phone number into WhatsApp on their own handset, pressed "forgot password" on your email, or logged in to your bank with a password leaked from another site. The service then texts you the final key. Once you read it out or forward it, they enter it within the few minutes it stays valid, change the password and recovery details, and you are locked out. With a bank, the same digits may approve a payment or add your card to their phone's wallet.

One rule covers every version: a code is typed only by you, into the app or website you opened yourself, for something you started. Nobody who phones, texts or messages you needs it, including staff, friends and buyers. The single exception runs the other way round. If you rang a company on a number you looked up, it may text a code to confirm who you are. On a call or chat that came to you, there is no safe reason to share one, and the wording of the text itself usually says so.

howItWorks.title: Your number or password is obtained
howItWorks.detail: The criminal starts with your mobile number from a marketplace advert, a contact list inside a hacked account, or a password exposed when another website was breached.

howItWorks.title: They trigger a genuine code
howItWorks.detail: They begin a login, password reset or new-device registration in your name. The real company's system responds by texting a one-time code to your phone.

howItWorks.title: A cover story arrives
howItWorks.detail: Within moments a call or message explains the code away: a security check, proof that you are a real seller, or a friend's mistyped number.

howItWorks.title: You pass the digits on
howItWorks.detail: Reading the code aloud or forwarding the text hands over the one thing they lacked. They type it in while you are still on the line.

howItWorks.title: The account changes hands
howItWorks.detail: The password, recovery email and phone number are swapped, your sessions are signed out, and the account is used to message your contacts or move money.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Priya, a physiotherapist, was between appointments when a WhatsApp message came in from Hannah, a friend from her running club. "Sorry, I sent my verification code to your number by accident. Can you forward it?" A text with a six-digit WhatsApp code had arrived a moment earlier, so the request seemed to fit. She had her thumb on the forward button when she read the rest of the text, which told her not to share the code with anyone. A code sent to her number could only be for her own account.

She rang Hannah instead of replying. Hannah had no idea what she meant, then discovered she had been logged out of WhatsApp that morning after forwarding a code to another club member. Priya ignored the request, warned the running group by ordinary text, and switched on two-step verification in WhatsApp's account settings so that a texted code alone would no longer be enough. Priya and Hannah are invented for this guide, but the chain of one hijacked account harvesting the next is how this scam spreads.

variations.name: The friend who mistyped
variations.detail: A hijacked WhatsApp or Instagram account messages its contacts asking them to forward a code "sent by mistake". Each person who obliges loses their own account, which then messages their contacts.

variations.name: Marketplace buyer verification
variations.detail: A buyer replying to your advert says they have been cheated before and will text a code to prove you are real. It is a Google Voice verification code, used to create a number linked to your phone.

variations.name: Bank fraud team call
variations.detail: A caller posing as your bank says a code will confirm your identity or cancel a payment. The text actually authorises a transfer, a new payee or a card being added to a mobile wallet.

variations.name: The fake support desk
variations.detail: After you complain publicly about a service, a lookalike support account replies offering help, starts a password reset on your account, and asks for the code "to locate your file".

realVsFake.real: A company texts a code only after a login, reset or payment has been started, and expects it typed into the same screen that asked for it.
realVsFake.fake: Someone contacts you to collect the code by voice, text or chat, so they can type it into a screen you cannot see.

realVsFake.real: Genuine code texts normally state their purpose, such as logging in or approving a payment, and many warn you not to share them.
realVsFake.fake: The caller's explanation contradicts the text, for example calling it a cancellation code when the message says it approves a payment.

realVsFake.real: Some firms do text a code to confirm your identity, but during a call you placed to their published number.
realVsFake.fake: The call came to you, from a number you cannot check, and the code is demanded before you can hang up and ring back.

realVsFake.real: A friend who mistypes a number simply requests another code to their own phone. A code sent to your number only works for your account.
realVsFake.fake: The "friend" insists the code on your phone belongs to them, needs it forwarded quickly, and avoids a voice call.

verify: Read the entire text before doing anything. Check which company sent it and what it says the code is for, then compare that with what you were told.
End the call and ring the number printed on your bank card or shown inside the company's own app. Ask whether any login or payment is waiting for approval.
If the request came from a friend, phone them on their usual number. An ordinary call reaches their real handset even when their chat account has been taken over.
Open the affected account yourself, change its password, and look at the list of logged-in devices or active sessions for any handset you do not recognise.
In WhatsApp, go to Settings, then Account, then Two-step verification, and set a PIN. For email and banking, switch from texted codes to an authenticator app where offered.

sharepoint-phishing-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The email looks like every other file notification you get at work. A blue "Open" button, a document name such as "Remittance Advice" or "Updated Contract", and the name of a supplier, client or colleague you really deal with. Often it truly is sent from that person's mailbox, because their account was taken over an hour earlier. Clicking brings up a Microsoft sign-in box with your organisation's logo. Nothing about it feels odd on a busy morning, since signing in to Microsoft several times a day is routine.

The sign-in box is the trap. Many of these pages sit between you and the real Microsoft login, passing your password and your authenticator approval through in real time and keeping the session token that Microsoft hands back. With that token the intruder opens your mailbox without needing your password or a second prompt. They read invoice threads, add inbox rules that hide replies, ask customers to pay into a different bank account, and send the same "shared file" notice to everyone in your address book. Your account becomes the next trusted sender.

The rule that stops it: never sign in on a page that an email opened for you. If a file has really been shared, it will be waiting when you open OneDrive or SharePoint from your own bookmark or the Microsoft 365 app launcher, already signed in. When you must check a page, read the address bar before typing. Your work password belongs only on Microsoft's own sign-in address, which for work accounts is login.microsoftonline.com, and on no other domain however exact the branding looks.

howItWorks.title: A trusted mailbox is hijacked
howItWorks.detail: Attackers first take over one real account, often at a supplier or client, and read through its sent items to learn who it normally exchanges documents with.

howItWorks.title: The share notice goes out
howItWorks.detail: Contacts receive a file notification naming a plausible document. Sometimes it is a genuine share of a file stored in the hijacked account's own OneDrive.

howItWorks.title: A button leads off-site
howItWorks.detail: The email button, or a "View document" link inside the shared file, opens a sign-in page on a domain that has nothing to do with Microsoft.

howItWorks.title: Credentials are relayed live
howItWorks.detail: Whatever you type is forwarded to the real Microsoft login as you type it, including your multi-factor approval, and the resulting session token is copied.

howItWorks.title: Your inbox is put to work
howItWorks.detail: The intruder searches your mail for invoices and payment threads, sets rules to hide warnings, and sends the lure onward from your address.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Tomasz handles accounts payable at a building supplies firm. On a Monday he received a SharePoint notice from Renata at a haulage company he pays every month: "Renata shared 'Statement and Remittance' with you". The button opened a Microsoft sign-in page showing his employer's logo. He had typed his email address and was reaching for the password when something nagged at him. Outlook was open in the next tab, already signed in, and the address bar showed a jumble of words ending in an unfamiliar domain rather than a Microsoft one.

He closed the tab and rang Renata on the number in the supplier record, not the one in the email signature. Her firm had found that morning that her mailbox was compromised and had been sending notices to every customer. Tomasz used the Report button in Outlook, and his IT team removed the same email from eleven other inboxes before anyone signed in. This is a fictional scenario, but the pattern of one breached supplier being used to reach its customers is typical.

variations.name: Genuine share, poisoned file
variations.detail: The notification is real and the file sits on a hijacked organisation's SharePoint. Inside is a single page with a blurred preview and a button leading to the fake login.

variations.name: QR code in the document
variations.detail: The shared PDF asks you to scan a QR code with your phone to view a secure message, moving you onto a personal device outside your employer's filtering.

variations.name: Device code request
variations.detail: The message supplies a short code and sends you to Microsoft's genuine device sign-in page. Entering it and signing in gives the attacker's machine access to your account, with no fake page involved.

variations.name: Permission request from an app
variations.detail: Instead of a password box, a prompt asks you to let an unfamiliar app read your mail and files. Clicking Accept grants lasting access that survives a password change.

realVsFake.real: Microsoft's work sign-in page loads on a Microsoft-owned address, and a password manager will offer to fill your saved login there.
realVsFake.fake: The page sits on an unrelated domain, so a password manager stays silent even though the logo and layout are copied exactly.

realVsFake.real: When you are already signed in to Microsoft 365 in that browser, a shared file normally opens straight away without asking for your password.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked for your password again although Outlook or Teams is open and working in another tab.

realVsFake.real: A file genuinely shared with your account also shows up in the Shared view when you open OneDrive yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The document can be reached only through the email button and appears nowhere in your own OneDrive or SharePoint.

realVsFake.real: The person named as sender recognises the file when you phone them or message them in Teams.
realVsFake.fake: A reply to the email is answered within minutes by whoever controls the mailbox, assuring you the link is safe.

verify: Hover over the button, or press and hold it on a phone, and read the domain it points to before opening anything.
Open OneDrive from the Microsoft 365 app launcher or your own bookmark and look in the Shared view. A real share from that sender will be listed there.
Phone the sender on a number from your contacts or supplier records. Avoid replying to the email, because the attacker may be the one reading the mailbox.
Use the Report button in Outlook to flag the message as phishing, or forward it to your security team, so copies can be pulled from colleagues' inboxes.
If you entered your password, tell IT at once and ask them to revoke your active sessions, then check Outlook's rules list for any you did not create.

irs-tax-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The phone rings, or a voicemail plays in a flat recorded voice: this is the Internal Revenue Service, a warrant has been issued, call back before officers are sent. The caller ID may read "IRS" or show a Washington area code. When you call, an agent gives a name and badge number, recites the last four digits of your Social Security number, and quotes an exact sum owed. Most people have some doubt about whether a past return was filed correctly, so the accusation lands on ground that already feels uncertain.

There is no tax case. The goal is a payment that cannot be reversed, collected before you speak to anyone else. You are kept on the line while you drive to a supermarket, told to buy gift cards and to tell the cashier they are presents, then asked to read out the numbers and PINs from the back. Other callers direct you to a wire transfer counter or a crypto cash machine. Once the first payment goes through, a new "penalty" or "lawyer's fee" appears, and the demands continue until you stop paying.

The rule is that tax is never settled on an incoming phone call. The real IRS normally opens a case with a letter sent through the post, gives you time to question or appeal the amount, and takes payment made out to the United States Treasury. It does not accept gift cards, and it does not send police to arrest people over a bill that same day. Hang up without discussing anything, then check your balance yourself through your IRS online account or by ringing the agency's published number.

howItWorks.title: A robocall leaves a threat
howItWorks.detail: Automated diallers leave voicemails about a warrant, lawsuit or suspended Social Security number, with a callback number that reaches the fraudsters' phone room.

howItWorks.title: The agent sounds official
howItWorks.detail: A caller gives a title, badge number and case reference, and may quote your address or partial Social Security number taken from leaked data.

howItWorks.title: A second call backs it up
howItWorks.detail: If you hesitate, another call arrives showing the number of your local police or sheriff's office, faked through caller ID spoofing, to confirm the warrant.

howItWorks.title: You are kept on the phone
howItWorks.detail: The agent insists you stay connected while you travel to buy gift cards or withdraw cash, and warns that telling anyone will violate a federal order.

howItWorks.title: Card numbers are read out
howItWorks.detail: You read the codes from the back of each card. The balance is drained within minutes, and a fresh fee is invented to keep you paying.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Lucille, a retired school cook, came home to a voicemail saying the IRS had filed a lawsuit against her and she should call a number before five o'clock. A man calling himself Officer Daniels answered. He read out her street address, said an audit had found 3,870 in unpaid tax, and told her the county sheriff would arrive within two hours unless she settled. He instructed her to drive to a pharmacy, buy gift cards in batches of 500, and keep her phone on speaker in her bag.

At the till the cashier asked whether someone on the phone had told her to buy the cards. That question broke the spell. Lucille left the cards on the counter, hung up, and at home called the IRS on the number printed in her old tax booklet. There was no balance and no lawsuit. She reported the call to the Treasury inspector general's office and told her bridge club about it. Lucille is a fictional character, though the script used on her is a familiar one.

variations.name: Refund waiting text or email
variations.detail: A message says a tax refund is ready and links to a copy of the IRS site. The form collects your Social Security number, date of birth and bank account details.

variations.name: Mailed lien letter
variations.detail: A letter from an invented "Bureau of Tax Enforcement" warns of a lien or levy and lists a toll-free number. The call centre demands immediate card or wire payment.

variations.name: Visa and deportation threats
variations.detail: Callers target recent immigrants and international students, sometimes in their first language, claiming an unpaid "federal student tax" or visa fee will lead to deportation.

variations.name: Other countries' tax agencies
variations.detail: The same script runs under the names of the Canada Revenue Agency and HM Revenue and Customs, swapping in a local arrest warrant and payment by e-transfer or vouchers.

realVsFake.real: The IRS normally starts with a letter delivered by the postal service, carrying a notice number you can look up on its website.
realVsFake.fake: First contact is a robocall, voicemail, text or email, with no letter ever having reached your address.

realVsFake.real: Tax payments go to the United States Treasury through the IRS's own payment options or a cheque made out to it.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to buy gift cards, wire cash to a named individual, or feed notes into a crypto machine.

realVsFake.real: A genuine bill sets out how the figure was reached and explains your right to question or appeal it.
realVsFake.fake: The amount must be paid within hours, and asking for paperwork is treated as refusing to cooperate.

realVsFake.real: IRS staff do not threaten same-day arrest by local police, or the loss of your driving licence or immigration status.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says deputies are already on their way and only immediate payment will recall the warrant.

verify: Hang up mid-sentence if you need to. Then sign in to your IRS online account from the agency's website, typed in yourself, to see any balance.
Call the IRS on 800-829-1040, its main line for individuals, and ask whether any notice has been issued against your name.
Look through your post for an IRS letter with a notice number in the corner. A phone demand with no earlier letter fits the scam pattern.
Report the call to the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration, and forward any scam email claiming to be the IRS to phishing@irs.gov.
If you have already read out gift card numbers, ring the issuer using the number on the card straight away and keep the cards and the receipt.

fake-pharmacy-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: It usually starts with an advert or a spam email at the moment you are weighing up a cost or an awkward conversation: a weight-loss injection your doctor will not prescribe, a painkiller repeat that has run out, tablets you would rather not ask for in person. The site has a white coat, a green cross and a row of trust seals. It offers the branded medicine at a fraction of the usual price, skips the prescription or replaces it with a short questionnaire, and promises plain packaging.

What arrives, if anything does, has not come through a licensed supply chain. Pills may hold the wrong dose, no active ingredient, or a different drug altogether, and injectables may have travelled unrefrigerated. Meanwhile the checkout has captured your card number, home address and the condition you were treating. Cards are charged again later under unrelated merchant names. Some buyers then receive a call from a supposed customs or drug-enforcement officer who says the parcel was intercepted and a fine must be paid to avoid prosecution, which is a second scam run from the same customer list.

The rule: buy prescription medicine only from a pharmacy you have found on the regulator's own register, and only against a prescription from someone who has assessed you. In Great Britain that register is kept by the General Pharmaceutical Council. In the United States, pharmacies are licensed by state boards of pharmacy, and the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy lists websites it has checked. A seller that will post a prescription-only drug to anyone who can pay is, by that fact alone, operating outside the system that keeps medicines genuine.

howItWorks.title: An advert meets a need
howItWorks.detail: Search ads, spam emails and social media posts promote in-demand medicines, often ones in short supply or embarrassing to request, priced well under what a registered pharmacy charges.

howItWorks.title: The prescription is waved away
howItWorks.detail: The site either states that none is required or shows a tick-box health form. No prescriber reviews it, and any answer leads to the checkout.

howItWorks.title: Checkout collects everything
howItWorks.detail: You supply card details, date of birth, address and medical history. Payment is sometimes switched at the last moment to bank transfer or cryptocurrency because "the card processor is down".

howItWorks.title: Something or nothing arrives
howItWorks.detail: Weeks later a padded envelope with an overseas postmark may contain loose blister strips or an unlabelled vial, with no leaflet, batch number or dispensing label.

howItWorks.title: Your details are reused
howItWorks.detail: The card is billed again for "refills" you did not order, your number is sold to other sellers, and fake officials may ring demanding a fine.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Derek, a taxi driver, had been told there was a long wait for the weight-loss injection his GP had mentioned. A sponsored post offered the same branded pen for 89, with "no prescription hassle". He answered six questions about his weight, typed in his card number, and received an order confirmation from an email address that did not match the site's name. Two days later his banking app showed the payment going to a merchant he had never heard of, in a foreign currency, followed by a second charge for the same amount.

The parcel came three weeks later: one pen in bubble wrap, warm to the touch, with a label in another language and no leaflet. Derek did not use it. He took it to his local pharmacist, who could find no batch number to check and advised him not to inject it. He rang his bank to dispute both charges and replace the card, and ignored a later call about a "customs fine". This account is illustrative and Derek is not a real person.

variations.name: The "Canadian" pharmacy front
variations.detail: A site decorated with maple leaves trades on Canada's reputation for cheaper medicine, while orders are filled from unregulated suppliers elsewhere and the business holds no Canadian pharmacy licence.

variations.name: Social media injection sellers
variations.detail: Accounts on social platforms and messaging apps sell weight-loss pens or vials labelled for "research use", take payment by bank transfer, and send products with no pharmacist involved.

variations.name: Cloned high-street brand
variations.detail: A copy of a well-known pharmacy chain's website, reached through an advert or a misspelt address, takes orders and card details that the real chain never sees.

variations.name: The fake agent follow-up
variations.detail: After an order, someone claiming to be a customs, drug-enforcement or medicines-agency officer phones to say you imported illegal drugs and must pay a penalty by wire transfer.

realVsFake.real: A registered pharmacy asks for a valid prescription, or has a named, registered prescriber assess you before anything prescription-only is supplied.
realVsFake.fake: Any prescription-only drug can be added to the basket by anyone, with at most a questionnaire that nobody reads.

realVsFake.real: Its registration or licence number matches an entry on the regulator's register showing the same business name and web address.
realVsFake.fake: Seals and badges are pasted in as images that link nowhere, or to a page the seller built itself.

realVsFake.real: Medicine arrives in the manufacturer's sealed box with a leaflet, batch number and expiry date, plus a dispensing label bearing your name.
realVsFake.fake: Loose strips or unmarked vials come in a plain envelope from overseas, with no leaflet and nothing naming a pharmacy.

realVsFake.real: A pharmacist can be reached by phone at a street address in your own country to answer questions about your order.
realVsFake.fake: Contact is a web form or chat window only, and payment by transfer, cryptocurrency or gift card is encouraged.

verify: Search the pharmacy's exact name on your regulator's register. In Great Britain use the General Pharmaceutical Council's register, and confirm the listed web address matches the one in your browser.
In the United States, check the site against the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy's list of verified websites, or look up the licence with your state board of pharmacy.
Ring the phone number shown on the site and ask to speak to the pharmacist. A registered pharmacy can put one on the line during opening hours.
Before paying, read who the payment is going to. Leave the page if you are asked to pay by bank transfer, cryptocurrency or gift card.
If a parcel has already arrived, leave the contents unused, take it with its packaging to a local pharmacist, and call the number on your card to dispute the charge.

deepfake-celebrity-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The clip appears as a sponsored post while you scroll: a household-name presenter, entrepreneur or money expert, apparently mid-interview on a real news set, explaining a trading platform that ordinary people are quietly using to earn a second income. The face is theirs because the footage is real, lifted from a genuine broadcast. Only the voice and the mouth movements have been regenerated to fit a new script. A banner along the bottom and a channel logo in the corner complete the impression that this was on television last night.

The video's only job is to get your phone number. The link opens a page dressed as a news article, where a form asks for your name, email and mobile. Within the hour an "account manager" calls, takes a starting deposit of around 250 by card, and shows you a dashboard where the balance climbs daily. The figures are typed in by the fraudsters. Larger deposits are coaxed out through calls and screen-sharing sessions, and when you ask to withdraw, a tax or release fee must be paid first. Nothing is ever returned.

The rule that defeats it: an endorsement counts only if you can find it on the person's own verified account or official website, reached by searching for them yourself. Well-known figures who have been cloned this way often post warnings saying they never promote investment schemes. Separately, no clip, however real it looks, changes what the platform is. Check the firm's name on your financial regulator's register before sending a penny, and treat any promise of fixed daily profit as the sign of a fraud.

howItWorks.title: Real footage is re-voiced
howItWorks.detail: Fraudsters take a genuine interview, clone the speaker's voice from public recordings, and use lip-sync software to make the mouth match a script about easy profits.

howItWorks.title: The clip runs as advertising
howItWorks.detail: It is placed as a paid advert from a newly created or renamed page, targeted by age and interests, and replaced with a fresh copy whenever it is taken down.

howItWorks.title: A fake news page follows
howItWorks.detail: The advert links to an imitation of a known news site. Every headline, menu item and comment on the page leads to the same registration form.

howItWorks.title: A call centre takes over
howItWorks.detail: A persuasive "adviser" phones, opens your account, takes a small first deposit and may ask you to install screen-sharing software so they can "guide" your trades.

howItWorks.title: Withdrawals hit a wall
howItWorks.detail: After weeks of invented gains and bigger deposits, a withdrawal request triggers demands for tax, commission or verification fees, and then the account and adviser disappear.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Callum, a self-employed plasterer, was eating lunch in his van when a video appeared in his feed. A consumer finance presenter he had watched for years seemed to be telling a breakfast show host about an automated trading tool that turned 250 into a monthly wage. He filled in the form underneath. A man with a polished manner rang twenty minutes later, took 250 from his debit card, and by Friday the dashboard showed 612. The adviser then proposed moving 5,000 in and asked him to install a remote-access app.

The request to control his phone made Callum pause. That evening he searched for the presenter's own website and found a pinned notice stating that any advert using his face to sell investments was fake. The platform's name appeared on the regulator's warning list. Callum asked to withdraw his 250 and was told a release fee applied, so he stopped answering, rang his bank's fraud line and reported the advert. Callum and the presenter are fictional, but each stage is drawn from how these operations run.

variations.name: Crypto doubling livestream
variations.detail: A looped video of a tech founder speaking at a real event is broadcast as "live", with a QR code promising to send back double any cryptocurrency transferred to the address shown.

variations.name: Miracle health product
variations.detail: A cloned television doctor or actor appears to recommend weight-loss gummies or a joint remedy. The checkout enrols your card in recurring monthly charges that are hard to cancel.

variations.name: Fake news bulletin
variations.detail: A synthetic newsreader on a copied studio backdrop reports that a government-backed investment scheme has opened to the public, with a politician's cloned voice endorsing it.

variations.name: Personal video from a star
variations.detail: After you comment on a fan page, an account posing as the celebrity sends a short personalised video greeting, then asks for money for a private meeting, charity or membership card.

realVsFake.real: Public figures announce paid partnerships on their own verified accounts and official websites, where the post can be found by anyone.
realVsFake.fake: The endorsement exists only inside a sponsored post from an unrelated page with few followers and no history.

realVsFake.real: A broadcaster's interviews can be found on its own website or channel, with a date and a full programme around them.
realVsFake.fake: The "interview they tried to ban" appears only on a lookalike news page whose links all lead to one sign-up form.

realVsFake.real: Authorised investment firms appear on the financial regulator's register and do not promise guaranteed returns.
realVsFake.fake: An unregistered platform promises fixed daily profits from an "AI" or "quantum" trading system, starting from a small deposit.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate broker pays withdrawals to your own bank account and takes any charges out of the balance it holds.
realVsFake.fake: You must send fresh money for tax, commission or "liquidity" before a withdrawal can be released.

verify: Search for the celebrity's verified profile or official website yourself and look for the offer there. Many targets pin a warning about fake adverts.
Type the platform's name into your financial regulator's register and warning list, such as the FCA's in the UK or the SEC's in the United States.
Replay the clip and watch the mouth. Look for blurring around the lips and teeth, a voice that stays oddly level, and gestures that do not fit the words.
Tap the name of the page running the advert. Check when it was created, what it was previously called, and whether it has any connection to the person shown.
If you already gave your number, expect calls. Decline any request to install screen-sharing or remote-access apps, and ring your card issuer if you paid a deposit.

whatsapp-job-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: A WhatsApp message arrives from a number you do not know, often with an overseas dialling code. "Hello, I'm Emily from a recruitment agency. We received your CV and have a remote role, 30 to 60 minutes a day." The sender uses the name of a real recruitment firm or well-known brand, and the timing tends to coincide with a job search, so it seems plausible that your details were passed on. The work sounds harmless: rating products or liking videos on a platform to "boost visibility".

The first day genuinely pays. A "trainer" walks you through a set of tasks on a slick website, a commission balance builds, and a small sum reaches your bank or crypto wallet. Then certain tasks start to cost money. A "combination order" drives your balance negative, and you are told to top it up with your own funds to finish the set and collect a much larger commission. Each top-up is bigger than the last, paid in cryptocurrency or to personal bank accounts, and withdrawal stays locked until the next deposit. The early payout was funded by other victims.

The rule is one sentence long: an employer pays you, and you never pay an employer. Any job that asks you to deposit, recharge, top up or "clear a negative balance" in order to keep working or to withdraw wages is a theft in progress, however much the dashboard says you have earned. Real recruiters do not hire by chat message without an interview, and real companies do not pay strangers daily commission for pressing a button forty times.

howItWorks.title: A recruiter makes contact
howItWorks.detail: A message on WhatsApp, SMS or Telegram offers flexible remote work with daily pay, claiming your number came from a job board or a CV database.

howItWorks.title: A trainer takes over
howItWorks.detail: You are passed to a second contact who registers you on a task website, often styled after a real retailer or app store, and demonstrates the first tasks.

howItWorks.title: A real payout builds belief
howItWorks.detail: After one or two sets of tasks you withdraw a modest amount successfully. A group chat full of "colleagues" posts screenshots of far larger withdrawals.

howItWorks.title: Tasks begin to cost money
howItWorks.detail: Special orders appear that push the account into deficit. You must deposit to continue, with the promise that the deposit and commission come back together.

howItWorks.title: The balance is held hostage
howItWorks.detail: The final task never comes. New conditions appear, such as a tax, a credit score repair or an upgrade fee, until you run out of money or refuse.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Ngozi, a newly qualified bookkeeper looking for extra hours, replied to a WhatsApp message offering part-time "app optimisation" work. A trainer called Sofia added her to a website with a retailer's logo and showed her how to press "submit" on forty product listings. On day one her account showed 42 in commission and Sofia helped her withdraw it. On day three a "combination order" turned her balance to minus 135. Sofia explained this was lucky, since such orders paid five times the commission once the shortfall was cleared.

Ngozi paid the 135, then a further 460 when a second combination order appeared two tasks later. What stopped her was the payment screen. Each top-up went to a different private individual's bank account, never to a company. As a bookkeeper she knew no payroll works that way. She refused the third request, took screenshots of the chat and the website, reported the payments to her bank that evening, and blocked both numbers. Ngozi's story is a composite written for illustration.

variations.name: Video liking on Telegram
variations.detail: You are paid small sums to like or subscribe to videos and send screenshots, then invited into a "prepaid task" group where you must send money first to earn more.

variations.name: Product rating platforms
variations.detail: A website imitating a shopping or app marketplace gives you sets of items to "optimise". Occasional bundled orders create a negative balance that only a deposit can clear.

variations.name: Hotel and travel review tasks
variations.detail: The platform borrows the branding of a travel booking site, and tasks involve "confirming" hotel bookings. Premium bookings require you to fund the reservation before commission is released.

variations.name: Payment processing assistant
variations.detail: The "job" is to receive transfers into your own bank account and forward them elsewhere for a cut. This moves stolen money and can lead to your account being closed.

realVsFake.real: A genuine recruiter names a specific vacancy, emails from the company's own domain and arranges an interview before any offer.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger offers work in the first message, hires you within minutes and conducts everything by chat.

realVsFake.real: Employers pay wages into your bank account through payroll, with a contract, a payslip and tax deducted.
realVsFake.fake: Earnings exist as a number on a website and are paid, if at all, in cryptocurrency or from private accounts.

realVsFake.real: A real job never requires you to put your own money into a work account to keep going.
realVsFake.fake: You must "recharge" to clear a deficit, and the request cannot be met from the commission you have supposedly earned.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate companies do not hire the public by chat app to rate products they have never used.
realVsFake.fake: The entire job is clicking a button on a list of items, which no business would need to pay for.

verify: Find the company's careers page through a search engine and contact its HR team by the email or phone listed there to ask whether this recruiter exists.
Check the dialling code of the number and whether the WhatsApp profile is a business account. A personal profile on a foreign number does not fit a local agency.
Ask for a written contract, the registered company number and a video interview. Watch whether the answers stay vague or the subject changes back to tasks.
When asked to top up, tell them to deduct it from your earned commission. A refusal confirms the balance on screen is not real money.
Open the chat, tap the contact's name, scroll down and use Report and Block. Then send your bank the payee details of any transfer you have already made.
