fake-giveaway-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: A direct message pops up minutes after you comment on a brand's competition post: "Congratulations! You have been chosen as our winner. Tap the link to claim your prize." The account has the brand's logo and almost the same handle, perhaps with an extra underscore or the word "winners" added. Because you really did enter something, the win feels earned. Other versions arrive cold by text or as a tagged comment, announcing a phone, a supermarket voucher or cash from a competition you do not remember, with a deadline measured in hours.

There is no prize, and the claim page reveals what the sender wants. Some ask for a small postage or "verification" payment, which hands over your card number and often signs you up to a recurring charge buried in the small print. Some display a copy of the Instagram or Facebook login screen and take over your account to send the same message to your followers. Others request your address, date of birth and a code texted to your phone, or tell you to send a little money through a payment app to "confirm your account" before the winnings are released.

The rule: a real prize costs nothing to receive and never needs your password. Genuine promotions announce winners from the official account that ran the competition, under published terms, and do not ask you to pay postage, tax or a release fee to the organiser. If a message about a win asks for a card number, a login, a texted code or any payment, it has answered its own question. Go to the brand's official page by searching for it yourself and see whether the result is posted there.

howItWorks.title: A real contest is shadowed
howItWorks.detail: Scammers watch genuine competitions run by brands and influencers, then create a duplicate profile using the same picture and a handle that differs by one character.

howItWorks.title: Entrants are messaged
howItWorks.detail: Everyone who commented on the real post receives a follow request and a message from the duplicate announcing they have won, usually with a short claim deadline.

howItWorks.title: A claim page opens
howItWorks.detail: The link leads to a form or login screen in the brand's colours. It asks for delivery details first, so the later request for card or password feels routine.

howItWorks.title: The small fee is taken
howItWorks.detail: A postage charge of a few pounds or dollars goes through. The terms hidden below the button authorise larger repeat payments to an unrelated merchant.

howItWorks.title: Your account recruits others
howItWorks.detail: If you entered your social media password, the profile is taken over and used to tag and message your friends with the same prize announcement.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Sione, an apprentice electrician, commented on a trainer brand's post offering a pair of limited-edition shoes. Within the hour he had a follow request and a message from an account with the brand's logo: he had won, and needed to confirm delivery within 24 hours. The link opened a tidy form. After his name and address it asked for 4.95 postage and his card details. He had typed the first four digits when he decided to look at the profile that had messaged him.

It had 83 followers, no posts, and a handle ending in an extra full stop. The brand's real page, which he found by searching, had a blue tick, a far larger following and a story stating that winners would be announced publicly and never asked to pay. Sione closed the form, reported the copy for impersonation through the profile menu, and warned two friends who had received the same message. He is an invented character, and the example is here to show the usual sequence.

variations.name: Share-to-win page posts
variations.detail: A page claims to be giving away returned campervans, laptops or boxes of supermarket vouchers to people who share and comment. Commenters then get a reply linking to a "registration" site.

variations.name: Free prize, postage only
variations.detail: A text or advert says you have won a phone or gift card and need only cover delivery. The card form enrols you in a costly subscription.

variations.name: Send-to-receive cash giveaways
variations.detail: An account posing as a celebrity or payment app promises to multiply money sent to it, or asks for a small transfer to "verify" your account before paying out.

variations.name: Hacked friend's prize tag
variations.detail: A friend's compromised profile tags you in a post about a prize draw they supposedly won. The link asks you to log in to vote or claim your share.

realVsFake.real: Genuine promotions contact winners from the same official account that ran the competition, and usually announce the result publicly.
realVsFake.fake: A separate profile with a near-identical handle, few followers and no posting history sends the winning message.

realVsFake.real: A real organiser covers delivery and does not ask winners to pay postage, tax or fees to release a prize.
realVsFake.fake: A small charge is requested by card, payment app or gift card before the prize can be "dispatched".

realVsFake.real: Claiming a real prize never involves typing your social media password or a texted security code into a form.
realVsFake.fake: The claim link opens a copy of the platform's login page, or asks for the code just sent to your phone.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate competitions publish terms stating who the promoter is, the closing date and how winners are picked.
realVsFake.fake: No terms exist, the closing date is "today", and you are told you won a draw you never entered.

verify: Open the profile that messaged you and compare its handle with the official account letter by letter. Check follower numbers, post history and the date it joined.
Search for the brand yourself, go to its verified page, and look for the competition post, its terms and any announcement of winners.
Scroll to the bottom of any claim page and read the small print beside the payment button for mention of a trial, membership or monthly charge.
If you paid a fee, call the number on your card, ask for any recurring payment to be stopped, and check your statement for later charges.
Report the copycat from its profile menu by choosing the option for an account pretending to be someone else, then tell the real brand.

pig-butchering-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: It begins with something small and human. A text meant for someone else: "Hi Anna, is the vet appointment still at four?" Or a match on a dating app with an attractive professional who lives abroad for now. You reply, they apologise or laugh, and a conversation starts that continues every day for weeks. Good morning messages, photos of dinner, questions about your family. They never ask for money, which is the detail that sets this apart from older romance frauds and persuades people that the relationship is sincere.

Eventually they mention how they afford their lifestyle: an uncle who is an analyst, a trading method, a platform. They offer to teach you, never to take your money themselves. You buy cryptocurrency on a genuine exchange, then send it to the website or app they recommend, where a dashboard shows it growing. That dashboard is a display the criminals control, and the coins left your possession the moment you transferred them. A small early withdrawal works, deposits grow, and when you try to cash out the account is frozen pending a "tax" that must be paid with new money.

The rule: never put money on a trading platform because someone you have not met in person suggested it, no matter how long you have talked or how much the screen says you have made. A balance is only real once it is back in your own bank account. Any platform that demands a further payment before releasing funds, instead of deducting it, is not holding your money at all. The kindest person in your phone can still be working from a script.

howItWorks.title: An accidental hello
howItWorks.detail: Contact starts with a misdirected text, a dating match or a friendly comment on social media. The profile photos, taken from a real person's account, show a comfortable life.

howItWorks.title: Weeks of daily contact
howItWorks.detail: The conversation moves to WhatsApp or Telegram and becomes a routine of messages and voice notes. Video calls are avoided or kept brief with excuses about work.

howItWorks.title: The investment is introduced
howItWorks.detail: They share screenshots of trading profits and credit a relative's inside knowledge. You are invited to try a small amount with their coaching.

howItWorks.title: Deposits grow on a fake exchange
howItWorks.detail: You send cryptocurrency from a real exchange to their platform. The displayed gains, a successful test withdrawal and time-limited "bonus events" encourage far larger transfers, sometimes from loans.

howItWorks.title: The exit is blocked
howItWorks.detail: A withdrawal request freezes the account. Support demands taxes or a security deposit, the friend urges you to pay, and after the last payment both go silent.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Greta, a dental hygienist who had divorced the year before, answered a text asking whether Saturday's tennis lesson was still on. The sender, Wei, apologised for the wrong number and they kept chatting. Over six weeks he sent photos of his dog, remembered her daughter's exam dates and talked about retiring early through short-term gold contracts his aunt had taught him. He guided her through buying 500 of cryptocurrency and moving it to a trading site. A week later it showed 780, and a withdrawal of 100 reached her bank.

She had moved 22,000 by the time she asked to take out 10,000 for a new roof. The site froze her account and asked for a tax payment sent separately. Wei told her to borrow it. That advice, from a man who claimed to care for her, was what she could not square. Greta searched one of his photos and found it on a stranger's profile under another name. She stopped paying, saved every chat, and reported to her bank and the police. Greta is fictional, and her story is a composite.

variations.name: Wrong-number friendship
variations.detail: No romance is offered. A mistaken text turns into a friendly acquaintance with a successful business owner who eventually shares a trading opportunity as a favour between friends.

variations.name: Liquidity mining wallets
variations.detail: You keep your coins in your own wallet app but open their link inside it and approve a "mining pool" contract. That approval lets them empty the wallet later.

variations.name: Investment group chats
variations.detail: You are added to a chat group run by a "professor" and an assistant, where members post winning trades. Most members are accounts run by the same operation.

variations.name: Fake apps outside the store
variations.detail: The platform is an app installed through a testing link or a downloaded profile instead of the official app store, which avoids the store's review and removal process.

realVsFake.real: Regulated brokers and exchanges can be found on a financial regulator's register under the same name and web address.
realVsFake.fake: The platform is known only through the person who introduced it, and its address differs slightly from a real exchange's.

realVsFake.real: A genuine exchange takes its fees out of the amount you withdraw and pays the remainder to your bank or wallet.
realVsFake.fake: Withdrawal is refused until you send a separate payment for tax, verification or a "risk deposit".

realVsFake.real: Someone who cares about you accepts a no, will meet or video call at length, and has no stake in where you invest.
realVsFake.fake: The contact dodges live video, steers every chat back to trading, and becomes hurt or angry when you hesitate.

realVsFake.real: Real investment values fall as well as rise, and no licensed adviser coaches clients through a chat app using a relative's tips.
realVsFake.fake: Every coached trade wins, the account never has a losing week, and bigger deposits unlock special "events".

verify: Save two of their profile photos and run a reverse image search. Stolen pictures often turn up under a different name on someone else's social media.
Ask for a live video call today, at a time you choose, lasting several minutes. Note whether it happens or yet another excuse appears.
Search the platform's exact web address together with the word "scam", and check your financial regulator's warning list for the name.
Look at how the trading app was installed. One that came from a link or a testing tool, not the official app store, has not been vetted.
Contact the genuine exchange where you bought the cryptocurrency through its own app, give them the receiving wallet address, and ask them to flag it.

family-emergency-text-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The message opens with "Hi Mum" or "Hi Dad" from a number your phone does not recognise. The sender says their handset went down the toilet or was smashed, that this is a temporary number, and that you can delete the old one. Nothing is asked of you at first. A few friendly lines go back and forth, often on WhatsApp, where the blank profile picture seems to fit the story of a replacement phone. It convinces because parents answer their children without thinking, and because your reply ("Is that you, Jamie?") usually hands over the name the sender needed.

The request comes an hour or a day later. An invoice, a rent payment or a new laptop has to be paid for today, and the banking app will not work on the replacement phone until a security check finishes. You are sent a sort code and account number, or an e-transfer address, in the name of a stranger described as a landlord, a supplier or a friend. That account belongs to a money mule, and whatever lands there is moved on within minutes. If the first payment goes through, a second bill tends to appear, usually larger than the first.

One rule stops it: no money moves until you have heard your child's voice on the number you already had for them. Ring the old number. It will usually ring as normal and your real son or daughter will pick up, puzzled. If the sender insists calls are impossible, ask for a voice note or a ten-second video call instead. Somebody who can type long messages about an urgent bill but can never speak a single word is working from a script, and the script has no answer for a parent who simply phones.

howItWorks.title: The new-number opener
howItWorks.detail: A text or WhatsApp message greets you as Mum or Dad, blames a broken or lost phone, and asks you to save this number. It names nobody, so it fits any parent who receives it.

howItWorks.title: You supply the name
howItWorks.detail: Replying "Is that you, Sophie?" tells the sender which child to play. From then on they sign off as Sophie and copy the affectionate tone you used.

howItWorks.title: Small talk, then a bill
howItWorks.detail: After some chat about the phone, they mention a payment due today and say online banking is locked for 48 hours while the new device is registered.

howItWorks.title: A stranger's account details
howItWorks.detail: You receive a payee name, sort code and account number, or an e-transfer email, with a promise of repayment tomorrow. The account belongs to a mule recruited to pass money on.

howItWorks.title: A second bill follows
howItWorks.detail: Once a payment clears, another expense appears, often bigger. The messages stop only when you refuse, call the real number, or your bank blocks a transfer.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: This invented example follows Moira, a retired school cook, who got a WhatsApp message on a Tuesday afternoon: "Hi Mum, phone's broken, this is my temporary number x". She assumed it was her son Callum, who works away on building sites, and said so. "Callum" explained that he owed a plant-hire firm 1,480 by five o'clock and could not get into his banking app on the borrowed phone. He sent account details for a payee called R Hale Services and promised to pay her back on Friday.

Moira typed the details into her banking app. A warning appeared saying the payee name did not match the account. That made her pause, and she noticed something else: Callum never signed off with an x. She pressed call on the new number and it rang out. Then she rang his old number and he answered from the site canteen, phone intact. She blocked and reported the sender in WhatsApp, sent a screenshot to her daughter so she would recognise the same script, and told her bank what had happened. No money left her account.

variations.name: Friend-in-need version
variations.detail: The same opener is sent as "Hey, it's me, new number" to reach people without children. It waits for you to guess a friend's name, then asks for a short loan.

variations.name: Grandparent phone call
variations.detail: A caller, sometimes crying, says "Grandma, it's me" and claims an arrest or car crash. A second voice posing as a lawyer or police officer then asks for bail money, often collected by courier.

variations.name: Cloned-voice call
variations.detail: A short recording that sounds like your relative says they are in trouble, then the line drops and the conversation continues by text. The voice is copied from clips posted on social media.

variations.name: Card photo request
variations.detail: Rather than a transfer, the sender asks for a photo of both sides of your debit card "so I can pay it myself", then asks you to read out the code your bank texts.

realVsFake.real: A child who replaces a broken phone normally keeps the same number, because the SIM or the mobile account moves to the new handset.
realVsFake.fake: The sender claims a new phone and a new number together, and suggests you delete the old contact.

realVsFake.real: A relative who needs help picks up when you ring, or calls back from a friend's phone or a landline.
realVsFake.fake: There is always a reason voice will not work: a broken microphone, poor signal, a meeting, a borrowed handset.

realVsFake.real: Family asking for a loan give their own bank details, which often already sit in your list of saved payees.
realVsFake.fake: The details belong to an unfamiliar name, explained away as a landlord, a supplier or a mate who is owed money.

realVsFake.real: Your actual child answers a personal question at once and is not offended that you checked.
realVsFake.fake: The impostor dodges, replies "Mum, I don't have time for this", or repeats that the bill is due today.

verify: Ring the number you already have saved for your child. A truly broken phone would go to voicemail, but the call is usually just answered.
Ask the sender for a voice note or a short video call. A replacement phone can still record audio, and the scammer will stall or refuse.
Put a question that social media cannot answer, such as what you cooked the last time they visited. Do not offer their name or any hints.
Look at the payee name you were sent. A bill for your child that must be paid to a private individual you have never heard of points to a mule account.
Forward the text to 7726, the spam-reporting short code used by mobile networks in the UK, United States and Canada, or use Report and Block on the chat in WhatsApp.

How to Recognize and Report Spam Text Messages

fake-subscription-renewal-email.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: An email thanks you for renewing a security or tech-support plan you do not remember buying. It carries an invoice number, a customer ID, and a charge of several hundred, said to be leaving your account today. There is often a PDF invoice attached and no link at all, only a line in bold: to cancel or dispute, call this toll-free number within 24 hours. Leaving out links helps it slip past spam filters, and the amount is pitched high enough to alarm you yet low enough to be believable for a multi-year plan covering several devices.

No charge exists. The phone number is the whole point, because it puts you on the line with a call centre that will offer a refund and ask you to install a remote-access app such as AnyDesk or TeamViewer so they can "process" it. With your screen under their control, they have you sign in to online banking, blank the display, and shuffle money between your own accounts or edit the page so it looks as if they refunded far too much. You are then begged to return the difference by gift card, wire or crypto.

The rule is that a charge is checked where charges actually live: on your card statement and in the account you hold with the real company, reached by typing its address or opening its app yourself. If nothing is pending there, the email has no hold over you and can be deleted. Cancelling a real subscription never requires a stranger to see your screen, and a real refund goes back to the card that was charged, leaving nothing for you to send anywhere.

howItWorks.title: A receipt for nothing
howItWorks.detail: The email poses as an order confirmation from a known antivirus or support brand, often sent from a free webmail address or through a real invoicing service so it looks authentic.

howItWorks.title: The call you place
howItWorks.detail: Because you dialled them, the agent sounds like customer service. They confirm the "order", ask for the invoice number, and say cancelling needs a short form on your computer.

howItWorks.title: Screen-sharing is installed
howItWorks.detail: You are walked through downloading a remote-access tool and reading out its session code. From that moment the agent can see and control everything on the machine.

howItWorks.title: The staged over-refund
howItWorks.detail: While your screen is blanked, they move your own savings into your current account or alter the figures on the page, then claim they typed 4,000 instead of 400.

howItWorks.title: Return the extra, please
howItWorks.detail: The agent pleads that their job is at risk and directs you to buy gift cards, wire funds, or feed cash into a crypto machine while staying on the phone.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: In this fictional example, Tomasz, a self-employed electrician, opened an email saying his three-year device protection plan had renewed for 389.99. He did have antivirus on the family laptop, so it seemed possible. He rang the number on the invoice. A polite agent found his "order", apologised, and asked him to download a small support tool to complete a cancellation form. Tomasz read out the nine-digit code on screen. The agent asked him to log in to his bank to confirm the refund had arrived, and the screen went black for a minute.

When the picture came back, his current account showed 3,890 extra. The agent gasped, said he had added a zero, and asked Tomasz to drive to a supermarket for gift cards to return the excess. Tomasz looked at his savings account first. It was lower by the same 3,890. Nothing had come in; his own money had simply been moved across. He shut the laptop lid, pulled the router cable, and called his bank from his mobile using the number on his card. The bank reset his online access, and he had the laptop checked and the remote tool removed.

variations.name: Payment-service invoice notice
variations.detail: An invoice or money request arrives through a real payment service, with the scam phone number typed into the seller's note field. The sending address is authentic, the claim is not.

variations.name: Home tech-support membership
variations.detail: The email names a retail repair service and a home-support plan. The callback script is the same, but ends with a request for card details to "reverse" the charge.

variations.name: Streaming or cloud-storage lapse
variations.detail: A message says your payment failed and the membership ends today, with an Update Payment button leading to a copied sign-in page that collects your password and card number.

variations.name: Cancellation form download
variations.detail: Instead of a phone number, the email links to a "cancel subscription" form. The file it downloads installs remote-access or data-stealing software without any call taking place.

realVsFake.real: A real renewal notice names the plan, usually shows the last digits of the card on file, and points you to your account to manage it.
realVsFake.fake: The fake gives an invoice number and a large total but no card digits, no account name, and one instruction: phone us.

realVsFake.real: Genuine companies send billing mail from their own domain, and the same charge appears as pending on your statement.
realVsFake.fake: This one comes from a free webmail address or a jumble of letters, and your banking app shows no matching transaction.

realVsFake.real: Cancelling a subscription you really hold is done in account settings or your phone's app store, with no software to install.
realVsFake.fake: The agent says cancellation requires a remote session and asks you to read out the access code shown on your screen.

realVsFake.real: An authentic refund returns to the original card automatically and shows up after a few working days.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to watch the "refund" arrive live in online banking, then told they overpaid and need money returned.

verify: Open your banking app and look at pending and recent card transactions. If the amount in the email is not there, no renewal has been charged.
Tap the sender's name to reveal the full address. A security company does not bill customers from a free webmail account or a misspelt domain.
Check subscriptions where they are actually held: your account on the company's own site, or the Subscriptions list in your phone's app store settings.
Use the Report phishing option in your mail app instead of replying, then delete the message. A reply tells the sender your address is read.
If a remote session is already open, switch off wifi or hold the power button, then call your bank from a different phone using the number on your card.

social-security-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The phone rings with a recorded voice: your Social Security number has been suspended because of suspicious activity, press 1 to speak to an officer. The caller ID may show the agency's real national number or a Washington area code, because both are easy to spoof. The person who picks up gives a name, a badge number and a case reference, then describes a car found near the Texas border, rented in your name, with drugs inside. It lands hard because the number is tied to your pension, your tax record and your credit, and few people have ever had cause to learn that it cannot be switched off.

Two things are being harvested. First the number itself, with your date of birth and bank details, "to verify the file", which is enough to open credit in your name. Then your savings. You are told your accounts will be frozen as evidence and that the only way to keep the money safe is to withdraw it and convert it: gift cards read out over the phone, cash fed into a crypto machine, or a transfer to a "government-protected" account. A second caller posing as a federal agent often joins to add weight, and you are told to keep the line open and say nothing to bank staff.

The rule is short. The Social Security Administration does not suspend numbers, does not threaten arrest by phone, and does not take payment in gift cards, wire transfers, crypto or cash handed to a courier. When there is a real problem with your record, it normally writes to you first, and the letter gives you time and a way to respond. So the right move with any call that opens with a suspended number is to hang up mid-sentence, without pressing a key, and check with the agency yourself.

howItWorks.title: The suspension robocall
howItWorks.detail: An automated message says your number is suspended or linked to a crime and tells you to press 1 or call back. Pressing anything shows the dialler that a person answered.

howItWorks.title: An officer with a badge number
howItWorks.detail: A live caller gives a title, badge number and case file, and may text a photo of an identity card or a letter on official-looking letterhead as proof.

howItWorks.title: The abandoned-car story
howItWorks.detail: You hear that a car, a bank account or a package tied to your number was used for drug trafficking or money laundering, and that a warrant is being prepared.

howItWorks.title: Confirming the nine digits
howItWorks.detail: To "clear" you, the caller asks for the full number, your date of birth, and which banks you use and roughly how much is held in each.

howItWorks.title: Savings moved for safekeeping
howItWorks.detail: You are kept on the line while you withdraw money and buy gift cards, use a crypto machine, or hand cash to a courier, with a promise of a new number and a refund.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Andre, a night-shift nurse, was woken at noon by a voicemail saying his Social Security number had been suspended and a warrant issued. This is an invented scenario, but the script is the common one. He called back. An "Officer Daniels" gave a badge number, said a car rented in Andre's name had been found abandoned in El Paso, and asked him to confirm his number to open a clearance file. Andre read out the last four digits. He was then transferred to a "marshal", who said his bank accounts would be frozen by evening unless the funds were secured.

The marshal told him to withdraw 2,400, buy gift cards at two different shops, and tell the cashier they were for family. That instruction to lie was what stopped him. No court he had ever heard of took fines in gift cards. He hung up, found the agency's number on its own website, and waited on hold to be told there was no case and no suspension. He reported the call to the agency's inspector general online, placed a fraud alert with a credit bureau because he had given part of his number, and let the next three callbacks ring out.

variations.name: Benefit increase offer
variations.detail: A friendly caller says you qualify for a cost-of-living rise or a one-off bonus and only need to confirm your number and bank details to activate it. Annual increases are applied automatically, without a call.

variations.name: Emailed statement notice
variations.detail: An email says your Social Security statement is ready to download. The button opens a copied sign-in page or installs software that gives the sender control of your computer.

variations.name: Badge and letter by text
variations.detail: After the call, a photo of a federal identity card or a letter with a seal arrives by text or email to back up the threat. Real officials do not send pictures of their credentials.

variations.name: Canadian SIN version
variations.detail: In Canada the same script names Service Canada or the border agency and says your Social Insurance Number is compromised, with payment demanded in Bitcoin or gift cards.

realVsFake.real: The agency's usual first contact about a problem is a mailed letter, and it mostly phones people who already have a claim or appointment in progress.
realVsFake.fake: The scam begins with a robocall or voicemail out of nowhere, giving you minutes to respond before "legal action".

realVsFake.real: Money owed to the agency is repaid through options set out in a mailed notice, which also explains how to question the amount.
realVsFake.fake: The caller wants gift card numbers read aloud, cash put into a crypto machine, or banknotes handed to a driver.

realVsFake.real: A genuine employee will not threaten you with arrest or tell you to keep a call secret from your bank or family.
realVsFake.fake: The "officer" says a warrant is active, tells you to stay on the line, and coaches you on what to say to the teller.

realVsFake.real: A Social Security number is not suspended, blocked or cancelled over the phone, and no fee exists to reactivate one.
realVsFake.fake: The script treats the number like a frozen bank card that unlocks once you pay or "verify" it.

verify: Hang up without pressing a key, then call the Social Security Administration yourself on 1-800-772-1213, the national number published on its official website.
Sign in to your my Social Security account by typing the agency's address yourself, and look for any notice or change on your record.
Check your post. A real issue with benefits or an overpayment arrives as a letter with a reference you can quote when you call the official number.
Disregard the caller ID. Scammers can make the agency's real number appear on your screen, so the display proves nothing about who is calling.
Report the call on the Office of the Inspector General's scam form, and if you gave your number away, place a free fraud alert with one credit bureau.

account-takeover-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: Often the first sign is small enough to ignore: a password-reset email you did not ask for, a text with a six-digit code at two in the morning, a notice that your account was opened on a Windows PC in a city you have never visited. Sometimes there is nothing at all until an app signs you out and your password no longer works. These notices are easy to wave away because they look like the routine noise every account produces, and because nothing appears to be missing yet.

Whoever is behind it wants to become you inside the account. They usually arrive with a password reused from a breached site, a login captured on a copied sign-in page, or a phone number moved to their own SIM. Once in, they change the recovery email and phone, add their own authenticator, and set a mail filter that hides security alerts. A shopping account yields saved cards and loyalty points. A bank login yields a new payee. An email account yields every reset link for everything else, plus a contact list to phish under your name.

The defence rests on one order of operations: secure the email account first, from a device you trust, before touching anything else. Change its password to one used nowhere else, sign out every other session, check the recovery details and forwarding rules, and turn on two-step sign-in. Only then work outward to bank, shopping and social accounts. Resetting those first is wasted effort if the intruder still reads the inbox where each new reset link arrives.

howItWorks.title: Credentials are obtained
howItWorks.detail: The password comes from a breach of another site where you used the same one, a phishing page, or malware that copies saved logins and browser sessions.

howItWorks.title: A quiet first login
howItWorks.detail: The intruder signs in, often through automated tools that test stolen passwords across many sites, and looks around without changing anything that would alert you.

howItWorks.title: Recovery details are swapped
howItWorks.detail: They replace your backup email and phone with theirs, add a new sign-in method, and may generate fresh backup codes so a password change alone will not remove them.

howItWorks.title: Alerts are buried
howItWorks.detail: In email, a filter or forwarding rule sends messages containing words like "security", "order" or "password" to the archive or to an outside address.

howItWorks.title: The account is cashed out
howItWorks.detail: Saved cards are used, points and gift balances are spent, payees are added, or your contacts receive a request for money that appears to come from you.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Nadia, a university administrator, noticed a password-reset email from a clothing retailer on a Sunday night and deleted it. Three days later a courier texted her mobile to say a parcel was out for delivery to a locker across town. She had ordered nothing. Her shop password no longer worked. When she looked in her email, there was no order confirmation and no "your details have changed" message, which seemed stranger than the parcel. This scenario is fictional, though each step in it is typical.

She opened her mail settings on her work laptop and found a filter she had never made, sending anything from the retailer straight to the bin, and a forwarding address ending in a string of numbers. The email password was one she had used on an old forum. She changed it, deleted the filter and the forwarding address, signed out all other sessions, and turned on two-step sign-in. Then she recovered the shop account, removed the saved card and the locker address, and rang her card issuer to dispute the order and replace the card.

variations.name: SIM swap or port-out
variations.detail: The criminal persuades your mobile network to move your number to their SIM. Your phone drops to no service, and every texted login code now goes to them.

variations.name: Sign-in prompt bombing
variations.detail: With your password already in hand, they trigger approval prompts on your phone again and again, sometimes followed by a call from "IT support" asking you to tap Approve.

variations.name: Real-time phishing relay
variations.detail: A copied sign-in page passes your password and one-time code to the real site as you type them, logging the attacker in before the code expires.

variations.name: Stolen browser session
variations.detail: Malware hidden in a pirated program or fake update copies the cookies that keep you signed in, letting the thief open your accounts without a password or code.

realVsFake.real: A genuine reset email is sent only because someone entered your address on the reset page. Ignore it and the password stays the same.
realVsFake.fake: A phishing version says the account will be locked today and links to a sign-in page that asks for your current password.

realVsFake.real: Real providers list sign-in history, devices and recovery details inside your security settings, where you can remove anything unfamiliar.
realVsFake.fake: The intruder relies on you never opening that page, and hides the provider's warning emails with a filter.

realVsFake.real: A one-time code or approval prompt is generated when a sign-in is attempted, and the provider does not ring to ask for it.
realVsFake.fake: A caller claiming to be the fraud team says a code has been sent to confirm your identity, and asks you to read it out.

realVsFake.real: When a recovery email or phone is changed, most providers notify the old address so the owner can object.
realVsFake.fake: The thief makes the change late at night, deletes the notice from your inbox, and hopes you find out too late.

verify: Open your email security page and read the list of signed-in devices. Sign out any phone, computer or location you do not recognise, then change the password.
In Gmail, check the Filters and Blocked Addresses tab and the Forwarding tab in settings. In Outlook, look under Rules and Forwarding. Delete anything you did not create.
Confirm the recovery email and recovery phone still belong to you. If either has changed, start the provider's official account recovery form straight away.
Glance at your phone's signal. If it shows no service or SOS only for no clear reason, call your mobile network from another phone and ask whether your number was moved.
Search the Sent, Bin and Archive folders for "reset" and "order". Messages you never saw reveal which other accounts were touched.

disconnection-threat-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: A caller says they are from the disconnections team at your electricity or gas company. Your last two payments failed, the account is in arrears, and a technician is already scheduled to cut the supply within the hour. The caller ID may show the company's name. The timing is rarely random: restaurants hear it just before the dinner rush, households on a freezing evening or a Friday afternoon when offices are about to close. With food in the fridge, a dining room full of customers or a child at home, checking the claim feels like a luxury there is no time for.

The caller wants a payment that cannot be pulled back. They quote an exact overdue figure, say the normal payment system is "locked" because of the pending disconnection, and send you to a shop for prepaid cards or gift cards, whose numbers you read out. Others give a bank account or payment-app handle, or direct you to a crypto machine. Some offer a callback number that plays the real company's hold message, copied to sound right. Card details taken "to stop the order" are used or sold afterwards, and people who pay once are called again about a "reconnection deposit".

What defeats it is your own bill. Hang up, find a paper or emailed statement, and ring the customer service number printed on it, or open the supplier's app and read the balance. Energy companies do not cut supply an hour after a first phone call. Disconnection for debt comes at the end of a string of written reminders and notices, and it is never cancelled by reading gift card numbers to someone on the phone. If the account shows nothing overdue, the call was theatre.

howItWorks.title: A crew is on its way
howItWorks.detail: A caller or text gives a deadline of thirty to sixty minutes and says a field technician has the work order. The short window is designed to rule out checking.

howItWorks.title: An exact amount owed
howItWorks.detail: They quote a precise figure such as 498.60 and a fake order number. The precision sounds like a billing system, though the caller cannot state your account number.

howItWorks.title: Normal payment is blocked
howItWorks.detail: You are told the website and app cannot accept payment on a flagged account, so the only way to stop the crew is a special same-day method.

howItWorks.title: Sent out to buy cards
howItWorks.detail: The caller stays on the line while you travel to a shop, buy prepaid or gift cards, and read the numbers aloud. Some send a QR code for a crypto machine.

howItWorks.title: The reconnection deposit
howItWorks.detail: After payment, a "supervisor" rings to say it failed to post, or that a deposit or new meter charge is now due, and the cycle repeats.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Linh runs a small noodle restaurant, and in this illustrative scenario the call came at ten to five on a Friday. The man said he was from the electricity company's disconnection desk, that two payments had bounced, and that a technician would shut off the meter at half past five unless 612.40 was paid. He gave an order number and a direct line to call back. With forty covers booked and a walk-in fridge full of stock, Linh took the cash float and started towards the pharmacy next door, where he had told her to buy prepaid cards.

At the door she stopped. Her bills were paid by direct debit, and she had never been asked to pay anything in a pharmacy. She went back to the office, pulled last month's statement from the folder, and rang the number at the top. The real company found her account in credit and no work order. The caller phoned twice more during service and she let it ring. Later she reported the number to the supplier's fraud team and told the cafe owners on her street, two of whom had received the same call that week.

variations.name: Meter replacement deposit
variations.detail: The caller says your meter is faulty or out of date and must be swapped today. A refundable deposit is demanded up front, or the supply will be shut off for safety.

variations.name: Overpayment refund call
variations.detail: You are told you overpaid and are owed money back. To send the refund, the caller needs your bank login or card number, which is the real goal.

variations.name: Pay-now text link
variations.detail: A text warns of a missed payment and links to a copied bill-payment page. It collects your card details and account login, with no caller involved.

variations.name: Doorstep disconnection visit
variations.detail: Someone in a hi-vis vest with a lanyard says they are here to cut the supply unless the debt is settled on the spot, by cash or a handheld card reader.

realVsFake.real: A real supplier sends reminders and a written disconnection notice over days or weeks before any cut-off for debt.
realVsFake.fake: The scam compresses the whole process into one phone call and a deadline measured in minutes.

realVsFake.real: Genuine staff can tell you your account number, your last payment date, and the amount on your latest bill.
realVsFake.fake: The caller knows your name and address at most, and deflects when asked for the account number.

realVsFake.real: Suppliers take payment through the methods listed on the bill, such as direct debit, card on their own site or app, or bank payment.
realVsFake.fake: The fraud insists on prepaid cards, gift cards, a payment-app transfer to an individual, or a crypto machine.

realVsFake.real: If you are behind, the company will discuss a payment plan and is content for you to call back on its published number.
realVsFake.fake: The impostor says hanging up will trigger the disconnection, and offers only a "direct line" that reaches the same crew.

verify: Find your latest bill or statement and compare the account number and balance with what the caller claimed. Ask them to read your account number first.
Hang up and dial the customer service number printed on the bill or shown in the supplier's app, never the one the caller or text supplied.
Log in to your online energy account. A real debt shows there as an overdue balance, alongside any bills or reminders already issued.
Check your bank statement for the last direct debit or card payment to the supplier. If it went through, the "failed payment" story is false.
If someone is at the door, keep it closed, ask for their ID number, and confirm it with the supplier's published phone line before any discussion.

online-task-job-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: A message arrives on WhatsApp, Telegram or by text from someone using the name of a real recruitment agency. They have a remote, part-time role: an hour or two a day "optimising" apps, rating products or liking videos, paid daily. No CV is requested. Say yes and you are passed to a "trainer" who sets you up on a slick platform carrying a known brand's logo. You click through a batch of tasks, a balance ticks upward, and a small payout really does reach you. That first withdrawal is the hook, and it is the most persuasive part of the whole design.

The platform is a prop, and the balance is a number on a web page the criminals control. Partway through a later task set, a "combination" or "premium" order appears that costs more than your balance and pushes the account negative. To continue, and to release what you have supposedly earned, you must top up the shortfall, usually by buying crypto such as USDT and sending it to a wallet address given by "customer service". Clear one, and a larger one follows. At the end come withdrawal taxes, verification deposits and penalties for "frozen" accounts. Every deposit is real money gone.

The rule that ends it: money in a job flows one way, from employer to worker. The moment any role asks you to deposit, top up, recharge or pay a fee in order to carry on working or to cash out, it is not employment, whatever the dashboard says. Treat the on-screen balance as fiction and count only what has actually left and entered your own bank account. Do not pay to rescue earlier payments. That urge to win back what you have already put in is exactly what each new demand is built to exploit.

howItWorks.title: A recruiter out of nowhere
howItWorks.detail: The first message cites a real staffing firm, says your number came from a jobs database, and offers flexible online work with daily pay and no interview.

howItWorks.title: Training with a demo balance
howItWorks.detail: A "trainer" sends a registration link and an invite code, then guides you through a set of clicks on a practice account so you watch commission add up.

howItWorks.title: A real early payout
howItWorks.detail: After the first set you withdraw a small sum, often in crypto. It costs the operators very little and exists to prove that the system pays.

howItWorks.title: The negative-balance order
howItWorks.detail: A special bundled task lands mid-set, priced above your balance. You cannot skip it, and the set must be finished before any withdrawal is allowed.

howItWorks.title: Fees to reach the exit
howItWorks.detail: When you ask to cash out, new conditions appear: a tax, a credit-score repair deposit, a fine for a "wrong operation". The trainer turns cold, then vanishes.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Rafael drives deliveries and wanted evening work. A WhatsApp message offered him app-rating tasks for an agency whose name he recognised, and a trainer called Mia walked him through forty clicks on a site styled like a well-known shopping brand. He withdrew 62 that night to his crypto app, and it arrived. On day three a "combination order" turned his balance to minus 180. Mia explained these were lucky, with five times the commission, and that he only had to clear the shortfall. He paid it. The next one was 540, then 1,300.

A Telegram group of "colleagues" kept posting screenshots of large withdrawals, which made him feel he was the one doing it wrong. What broke the spell was the withdrawal page: with his set finally complete, it asked for a further 900 as "tax", payable up front. He searched for the agency's real website, found a warning that it never recruits through messaging apps, and stopped. He screenshotted the chats and wallet addresses, reported them to his bank and the fraud reporting service, and blocked Mia. Rafael is an illustrative composite, not a real individual.

variations.name: Video-liking groups
variations.detail: You are paid a small amount per like or subscription, then invited into a Telegram group where "prepaid tasks" require sending money first for a promised higher return.

variations.name: Hotel and travel review boosting
variations.detail: The platform imitates a booking site and asks you to "rate" hotels or flights. Luxury packages appear as expensive bundled orders that must be funded from your own pocket.

variations.name: Order-grabbing for online shops
variations.detail: You are told to place pretend purchases to lift a seller's ranking, paying for each order yourself with a refund plus commission promised once the batch is complete.

variations.name: Recruit-a-friend bonuses
variations.detail: To unlock withdrawal or earn a bonus, you are pushed to bring in relatives using your invite code, which supplies the operators with fresh targets who trust you.

realVsFake.real: A genuine employer interviews you, issues a written contract, and takes tax and bank details through a proper onboarding process.
realVsFake.fake: The task job hires you in a chat within minutes and asks only for a phone number and an invite code.

realVsFake.real: Real wages arrive in your bank account on a stated payday and appear on a payslip.
realVsFake.fake: Here the "salary" is a figure on a dashboard, with payouts in crypto and only after conditions that keep changing.

realVsFake.real: A real business funds its own orders, marketing and stock. Staff are never asked to cover a shortfall.
realVsFake.fake: The platform sends "combination" orders that drive your balance negative, then demands a top-up before you may continue.

realVsFake.real: Agency recruiters write from a company email address and can be reached through the firm's switchboard.
realVsFake.fake: The scam recruiter uses a personal messaging account, often with an overseas country code, and avoids voice or video calls.

verify: Find the recruitment agency's real website through a search engine and use its contact page to ask whether this recruiter and vacancy exist.
Compare the platform's web address with the brand it claims to be. Task sites use look-alike names with extra words, hyphens or odd endings.
Search the platform name together with the words "task scam" or "withdrawal problem". Other people's reports tend to appear near the top of the results.
Ask the trainer for a video call and a contract naming a registered company and address. Watch how quickly the conversation is steered back to tasks.
Add up money that has actually moved in your bank or crypto app. If more has gone out than come in, stop sending and call your bank today.

sources.title: What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams

hacked-friend-help-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The message comes from someone you know, inside the same chat where you swapped birthday wishes last month. Their name, their photo and your whole history together are sitting right there above it. "Are you around? Need a quick favour." Nothing about the account is forged, which is why it works. Your friend's login was stolen, perhaps an hour ago, and a stranger is now working through their contact list. People are careful with unknown numbers and careless with familiar faces, and the opening line is kept vague so that you reply before any request has been made.

Three things are usually wanted. Money: a short loan because a banking app has hit its limit, sent to a third party's account, or gift cards for a niece's birthday with the codes photographed. A code: the six digits that have just arrived on your phone, described as theirs and sent to you "by mistake". In truth the scammer has started a login or reset on your own account, and reading it out hands that account over. Or a click: a link captioned "is this you?" that opens a copied login page. Each success gives them another real account to message from.

The rule is to move the conversation off the channel it arrived on. Phone your friend's mobile, or text the number you have saved, and ask whether they just messaged you. Do this before replying, paying or reading anything out. And treat any code that reaches your phone as yours alone: platforms send login codes to the account owner, so nobody else's code can turn up on your device by accident. A true friend will not mind a thirty-second call, and the impostor cannot take one.

howItWorks.title: Your friend is hacked first
howItWorks.detail: They entered their password on a fake page or shared a code, and the scammer now controls their profile, with access to chats, photos and the friends list.

howItWorks.title: An opener that asks nothing
howItWorks.detail: You get "hey, you busy?" or "can I ask a favour?" The scammer waits for a reply before going further, so effort is spent only on contacts who are awake and answering.

howItWorks.title: The request is tailored
howItWorks.detail: Past messages show how your friend talks to you. The scammer borrows nicknames and in-jokes, then asks for a loan, gift cards, or a code "sent to you".

howItWorks.title: Your code, their login
howItWorks.detail: Meanwhile they enter your phone number on the app's login or reset screen. The code you receive is the key to your account, and it goes to them.

howItWorks.title: Your contacts are next
howItWorks.detail: With your account captured, everyone you know gets the same messages under your name. Your friend, still locked out, cannot warn anyone through the app.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Siobhan, a nursery worker, got an Instagram message from her old flatmate Dee at eleven at night: "Hey, are you up? I'm locked out of my account on my new phone and it's sending the code to a trusted friend. Can you tell me what it says?" A text with a six-digit code landed seconds later. They had chatted in that thread only last week, and Dee was always losing things. Siobhan had the code copied and ready to paste. This is a fictional example built from the usual pattern.

Then she read the text properly. It named a messaging app, not Instagram, and ended with "do not share this code". Dee's message also said "kindly", a word she had never used. Siobhan rang Dee's mobile. Dee answered, half asleep, and said she had been locked out of Instagram since teatime after clicking a link about a competition. Siobhan deleted the code, reported Dee's profile as hacked, switched on two-step verification in her own apps, and posted a warning in their group chat. Two others had already been asked for money.

variations.name: Messaging-app code grab
variations.detail: The scammer registers your number on their own handset, which sends a six-digit code to you by SMS. A hijacked friend's account then asks you to forward it.

variations.name: Vote-for-me link
variations.detail: A friend asks you to vote for them in a contest or ambassador programme. The link opens a copied login screen, and whatever you type is used to take over your profile.

variations.name: Stranded or short of cash
variations.detail: The friend's account says they are stuck abroad or their card is blocked, and asks you to send money to another person's account or e-transfer address.

variations.name: Investment success post
variations.detail: The hacked profile posts a story about doubling money with a crypto "mentor" and replies to anyone curious, steering them to a fake trading site.

realVsFake.real: Platforms send a login or reset code only to the phone number or email registered on the account being opened.
realVsFake.fake: The message claims your friend's code landed on your phone "by mistake" and asks you to send it over.

realVsFake.real: A real friend in a jam will answer a call, or ring you back from someone else's phone within minutes.
realVsFake.fake: The impostor keeps to typed messages, says the signal is bad, and pushes for an answer before you can check.

realVsFake.real: When a friend borrows money, it goes to their own account or the payment handle you have used with them before.
realVsFake.fake: The hijacker names a stranger's account, a new e-transfer address, or asks for gift card codes sent as photos.

realVsFake.real: A video a friend really shares plays inside the app you are already signed in to.
realVsFake.fake: The scam link opens a page that asks you to log in again before you can watch.

verify: Call your friend's mobile number, or text it, and ask if they just messaged you on the app. Do not ask inside the same chat.
Read the code text in full. It names the service it came from and usually says not to share it, which tells you whose account it unlocks.
Ask the sender something that is not in your chat history, such as where the two of you first met, and see whether a straight answer comes back.
Message one mutual friend by another route and ask whether they received the same request. Hijackers send one line to many contacts at once.
In WhatsApp, open Settings, then Account, and turn on two-step verification so a leaked SMS code alone cannot register your number elsewhere.

crypto-recovery-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: It arrives when you are at your lowest. You have lost money to a fake trading platform or a drained wallet, and perhaps posted about it or filed a complaint. Then a message: a "blockchain forensics" firm, a law office, or someone claiming to work with a government agency has traced your funds to a holding wallet and can release them. There may be a case number, a tracing report with real transaction hashes, a website full of testimonials. It persuades because it says the one thing you most want to hear, and because the sender already knows what you lost.

That knowledge is the giveaway. Lists of people who have already paid a scammer are traded, and often the "recovery agent" belongs to the same group that took the money the first time. The aim is a second harvest. It starts with an upfront charge, called a retainer, gas fee, wallet activation or tax, paid in crypto so it cannot be reversed. Some ask instead for your seed phrase, or for you to connect your wallet to a "claims portal" that empties it. A dashboard may show your recovered balance, held just out of reach behind one more fee.

One rule covers every version: do not pay anyone who contacts you offering to get lost crypto back. Police, regulators and fraud reporting centres never charge to take a report or to return money, and they do not recruit through comments or direct messages. Crypto transfers cannot be reversed by a technician. Where funds are ever frozen, it happens through law enforcement and court orders served on an exchange, slowly and without guarantees. If someone found you, promises success, and wants a fee or wallet access first, you are looking at the second scam.

howItWorks.title: Finding people who lost
howItWorks.detail: Targets come from traded victim lists, from the original scammers' own records, and from public posts on forums and social media describing a loss.

howItWorks.title: The specialist introduces himself
howItWorks.detail: A message, comment reply or search advert presents a recovery firm, lawyer or agency investigator, complete with licence numbers, a case reference and a professional website.

howItWorks.title: A tracing report as proof
howItWorks.detail: You are sent a document showing your transactions on a block explorer and a wallet said to hold your funds. Anyone can look up that public data.

howItWorks.title: The activation fee
howItWorks.detail: Before release, a payment is required: a retainer, network gas, a wallet activation deposit or tax. It must be sent in crypto and inside a short deadline.

howItWorks.title: One more obstacle
howItWorks.detail: After payment, a new cost appears, such as an anti-money-laundering deposit or exchange release charge. Requests continue until you stop paying, then the contact disappears.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Yusuf, an IT contractor, had lost savings to a fake trading app and wrote about it on a forum. Within a day a reply recommended a "recovery specialist" who had helped the poster. On Telegram the specialist sent a tracing report with Yusuf's own transaction hashes and a screenshot of a wallet holding his coins. Release needed a refundable activation fee of 0.02 BTC within 48 hours. Yusuf knew the hashes were genuine, and he paid. Two days later a "compliance officer" wrote that an anti-money-laundering deposit was also due. This scenario is invented for illustration.

Before paying again he pasted the holding wallet's address into a public block explorer. It was a large exchange's deposit address, visible to anyone, with no link to his case. The hashes proved only that the specialist could read a public ledger. He then searched the firm's name on the regulator's register and found nothing. Yusuf stopped replying, saved the chats and addresses, and added the recovery approach to the police report he had already filed for the first loss. He told his bank as well, and changed the email password he had shared for "verification".

variations.name: Government or police impersonator
variations.detail: An email or call claims to come from a fraud agency, a regulator or a court-appointed fund, saying you are on a compensation list and must pay a processing fee to be included.

variations.name: Planted recommendation comments
variations.detail: Replies under posts about scams praise a named "ethical hacker" and give an Instagram handle or webmail address. The accounts posting the praise belong to the scammers.

variations.name: Wallet-drainer claims portal
variations.detail: You are sent to a site to "claim" recovered tokens and asked to connect your wallet or type your seed phrase. Approving the prompt lets them empty whatever remains.

variations.name: Fake law firm
variations.detail: A website copies the names and photos of real lawyers and offers a class action or asset recovery. The retainer is requested in crypto or by transfer to a personal account.

realVsFake.real: Police and official fraud reporting centres take your report for free and never ask for payment to open, speed up or close a case.
realVsFake.fake: The recovery agent needs an activation fee, retainer or tax, payable in crypto, before anything can be released.

realVsFake.real: Frozen funds are returned through a legal process involving law enforcement and the exchange, with no promised outcome or date.
realVsFake.fake: The scam guarantees your full balance back within days and shows it waiting on a private dashboard.

realVsFake.real: Tracing uses the public blockchain. A genuine investigator has no use for your seed phrase, private key or remote access to your device.
realVsFake.fake: The fraudster asks for the seed phrase or a wallet connection "so the recovered coins can be deposited".

realVsFake.real: Regulated law firms and investigators can be checked on a professional register and reached through listed office numbers.
realVsFake.fake: The impostor works from Telegram, a webmail address and a newly registered site, and discourages you from telling your bank or family.

verify: Scroll back to the first message and note who started the conversation. An offer that reached you by comment reply, direct message or cold call is the warning.
Paste any "holding wallet" address they quote into a public block explorer. Seeing coins there proves nothing about their power to move them.
Look up the firm or lawyer on the official register for your country, then phone the office number listed there instead of the one in the message.
Check that your seed phrase has never been typed into any site or chat. If it has, create a new wallet now and move remaining funds to it.
File the original loss with your national reporting centre: IC3 in the United States, Action Fraud in the UK, or the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. None charges a fee.

sources.title: What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams

data-breach-text-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The text says your account 'was found in a data breach' and gives you a link to secure it. It tends to arrive in the days after a real breach has been in the news, when your inbox may already hold a genuine notice from some other company, so the claim feels plausible before you have read to the end. Nothing in it names the service, the date or the data involved. That vagueness is deliberate: the same wording can be sent to every number on a list, and each reader fills in whichever account they worry about most.

The link opens a copy of a sign-in page, usually for an email provider, a bank or a big shopping account. You type your current password 'to confirm it is you', and the page hands it to the criminal. Many of these pages then ask for the six-digit code your real provider has just texted you. That happens because someone is signing in to the genuine site with your password at that moment, and the code is the last thing they need. Once inside, they change the recovery email and phone number so that you are the one locked out.

One rule defeats it: a breach warning is never a reason to sign in through the message that delivered it. If you are worried, close the text, open the app you already have or type the address yourself, and change the password there. A company that has really lost your data does not need your current password to tell you so, and it cannot make you safer by collecting it again. Treat any breach text that ends in a login box as the attack itself.

howItWorks.title: A bulk warning goes out
howItWorks.detail: Criminals send the same breach notice to a long list of mobile numbers, often timed to follow news coverage of a real leak so the claim sounds familiar.

howItWorks.title: The link imitates a login
howItWorks.detail: Tapping it opens a cloned sign-in page on a lookalike address, with the right logo and colours, built for a phone screen where the address bar is cut short.

howItWorks.title: Your password is captured
howItWorks.detail: Whatever you type into the username and password boxes is sent straight to the criminal, who tries it on the real service within seconds.

howItWorks.title: The code request follows
howItWorks.detail: The page asks for the one-time code your provider just sent. That code was triggered by the criminal's own sign-in attempt, and entering it lets them through.

howItWorks.title: Recovery email and phone change
howItWorks.detail: Inside the account, they change the recovery email and phone, set up mail forwarding, and try the same password on your other accounts.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: This example is fictional. Priya, a dental receptionist, had read that morning about a breach at a large ticketing company. At lunch a text arrived: 'Security notice: your account was found in a data breach. Verify now to prevent unauthorised access.' She assumed it was about her email, tapped the link and saw what looked like her provider's sign-in page. She typed her address and password. The next screen asked for the six-digit code that had just arrived by text from her real provider.

That second text is what stopped her. It read 'Your verification code is 418 205. Do not share it with anyone', and she realised she had not asked for a code. She closed the page, opened the email app already on her phone and changed the password from there, then signed out every other session in the security settings. She found one failed sign-in from another country. Because she had reused that password on a shopping site, she changed it there too, and forwarded the text to 7726.

variations.name: Breach compensation claim form
variations.detail: The text says you are owed a payout for a breach and links to a 'claim' form that collects your bank details, date of birth and photos of identity documents.

variations.name: Free credit monitoring enrolment
variations.detail: Posing as a breached company, it offers free monitoring and asks for a national insurance or social security number, which helps a criminal open credit in your name.

variations.name: Dark web password alert
variations.detail: Styled like a password manager or phone security notice, it claims your password was 'found on the dark web' and sends you to a fake reset page.

variations.name: Call-back breach helpline
variations.detail: Instead of a link there is a phone number. The 'security team' who answers asks you to install a remote access app so they can 'check your device'.

realVsFake.real: A genuine breach notice names the company, says roughly when the incident happened and lists which kinds of data were taken.
realVsFake.fake: The text says only 'your account' or 'your data', so it fits whichever service the reader happens to worry about.

realVsFake.real: Companies that reset passwords after a breach make you choose a new one the next time you sign in on their own site or app.
realVsFake.fake: The message asks for your current password on a page reached from the text, which protects nothing and hands it over.

realVsFake.real: A one-time code is sent only when someone starts a sign-in, and the message carrying it usually warns you not to share it.
realVsFake.fake: The fake page asks you to type that code in to 'complete verification', which finishes the criminal's own login.

realVsFake.real: Formal breach notifications usually come by email or letter to the contact details the company holds, and nothing in them expires within the hour.
realVsFake.fake: The text gives you minutes or hours and warns of 'imminent unauthorised access' to stop you checking anywhere else.

verify: Open the app for the account you think is affected and look at its security or login activity page for sign-ins and devices you do not recognise.
Type the company's address into your browser yourself and check its news or help page, where a real breach will be announced publicly.
Check your phone's built-in password manager, which flags saved passwords that have appeared in known leaks, and change any it lists.
Look at the address in the text without tapping it. A real provider's name followed by extra words, hyphens or an unfamiliar ending means the page is a copy.
Forward the text to 7726, the spam reporting number used by most carriers in the US, UK and Canada, then delete it.

sextortion-email-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The email opens with a password you recognise. It goes on to say that malware on your computer switched on the webcam while you visited an adult site, that the sender has the footage and your contact list, and that everyone you know will receive the video unless Bitcoin arrives within 48 hours. Sometimes the message appears to have been sent from your own address. Reading it alone, with a real password of yours on the screen, most people feel a jolt of doubt about what might have been recorded, and that jolt is the entire mechanism.

What the sender actually holds is a line from an old breach: your email address and a password you once used on some site that was later hacked. Lists like that are traded in bulk, and a script merges each line into the same template and sends it to everyone on the list. No device was infected and no video exists. The demand is for cryptocurrency because a transfer to a wallet address cannot be recalled by a bank. Anyone who pays is marked as a payer, and further demands tend to follow.

The rule is to pay nothing and send no reply. A blackmailer with a real recording would show a frame of it, because proof gets money faster than threats, and these emails never do. Treat the quoted password as a useful warning instead: if you still use it anywhere, change it there today and turn on two-step sign-in. Then report the email as phishing and delete it. The deadline in a mass-sent email like this passes quietly, because there was never anything to send.

howItWorks.title: Leaked passwords are bought
howItWorks.detail: The sender obtains a breach list pairing email addresses with old passwords, and sometimes phone numbers or home addresses, from sites that were hacked long ago.

howItWorks.title: A template is mail-merged
howItWorks.detail: Software drops each person's password into identical threatening text and sends it in bulk, often as an image or PDF so spam filters cannot read the words.

howItWorks.title: False proof is added
howItWorks.detail: The From line may be forged to show your own address, and the text claims a hidden tracking pixel has reported that you opened the message.

howItWorks.title: A countdown is set
howItWorks.detail: You are given one or two days to pay a fixed sum to a Bitcoin wallet address, with a suggestion to search online for how to buy cryptocurrency.

howItWorks.title: Payers get asked again
howItWorks.detail: People who pay often receive a second demand saying the price has risen. People who ignore it face no consequence, though the same template may arrive again.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Tomasz, a secondary school teacher, opened his personal email on a Sunday evening and found a message with one of his old passwords as the subject line. The sender claimed to have installed spyware through a 'compromised adult site', to have recorded him through his laptop camera, and to hold his full contact list. The price for silence was $1,200 in Bitcoin within two days. The email appeared to come from his own address, which the sender offered as proof of 'full access' to his account.

He noticed that the password was one he had used for a forum account and nowhere else for a long time. He checked his Sent folder, which showed no such message, and pasted a sentence from the email into a search engine, where the same wording appeared in posts from other recipients. He changed the two accounts that still shared a similar password, turned on two-step sign-in, marked the message as phishing and deleted it. The deadline passed without incident. Tomasz is an invented character, but this is how the scam typically runs.

variations.name: Email 'sent from your account'
variations.detail: The From field is forged to match your own address. Forging it takes no access to your mailbox, and your Sent folder will not contain the message.

variations.name: Home address and street photo
variations.detail: Newer templates add your postal address and a picture of your street copied from an online mapping service, both taken from leaked or public records.

variations.name: Fake police or court notice
variations.detail: A PDF on official-looking letterhead accuses you of viewing illegal material and demands a reply or a 'fine' to avoid prosecution.

variations.name: Real images from a chat
variations.detail: A different crime: someone you video-chatted with has actual screenshots and threatens to share them. Stop contact, keep the evidence, and report it to the platform and the police.

realVsFake.real: A blackmailer who truly held a recording would attach a still or a short clip, because proof is the quickest route to payment.
realVsFake.fake: The email describes a video in terms that could apply to anyone and never shows a single frame.

realVsFake.real: A message genuinely sent from your mailbox appears in your Sent folder and shows your provider's servers in its headers.
realVsFake.fake: Only the visible From line carries your address. The headers show an unrelated server, and Sent contains nothing.

realVsFake.real: A password exposed in an old breach opens only the site it was used on, and only if you never changed it.
realVsFake.fake: The email presents that old password as evidence of live control over your computer, camera and contacts.

realVsFake.real: Personal threats from someone who knows you mention names, places or events that only that person could know.
realVsFake.fake: Every recipient gets the same wording, with only the password, and sometimes a phone number, swapped in from a leaked list.

verify: Work out where the quoted password came from. If you still use it on any site, sign in there directly and change it now.
Open your Sent folder and your account's recent sign-in activity. No sent copy and no unfamiliar devices means nobody has been inside your mailbox.
Copy one distinctive sentence from the email into a search engine. Identical text posted by other recipients confirms it is a mass template.
Run a full scan with the security tool built into your computer if the malware claim worries you, and install any pending system updates.
Report the message with your email provider's 'Report phishing' option, keep a copy if you plan to tell the police, then delete it.
