military-romance-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The profile shows a man in uniform, often a sergeant or an army doctor, widowed, with a young child being cared for back home. He writes every morning and every night, uses pet names within days, and explains early that he is on a deployment where cameras are restricted and calls are monitored. That one detail does a lot of work: it accounts for the absent video call, the odd hours and the months before he can visit. The uniform supplies the trust. Few people feel comfortable doubting a soldier who says he is serving overseas.

The photos belong to a real service member who has no idea they are being used. The person typing is after a series of payments, each attached to a military-sounding reason: a fee to process a leave request, a 'replacement officer' charge, a satellite phone card, a flight home, customs clearance on a box of valuables he is sending ahead. Payment is asked for in gift card codes, wire transfers to a third-party 'agent', or cryptocurrency. Each payment produces a new obstacle, and the meeting moves back again.

The rule that ends it: no armed force charges a soldier, or a soldier's partner, for leave, travel home, medical care or phone access. Leave is approved inside the chain of command and involves no civilian paperwork and no fee. Serving personnel are paid into their own bank accounts and can reach that money while deployed. The first request for money therefore tells you who you are talking to, however long and affectionate the conversation has been.

howItWorks.title: A uniformed profile appears
howItWorks.detail: The account uses photos lifted from a real service member's public social media, with a rank, a unit and a sympathetic story about being widowed.

howItWorks.title: The chat leaves the app
howItWorks.detail: Within days he suggests moving to WhatsApp, Telegram or email 'for security', which takes the conversation away from the dating site's moderators and reporting tools.

howItWorks.title: Video calls are ruled out
howItWorks.detail: Deployment rules are blamed for every missed call. At most you receive voice notes, old photos or a few seconds of blurred video that freezes.

howItWorks.title: An official-looking fee arrives
howItWorks.detail: A 'commanding officer' or 'military finance office' emails a form from a free webmail address stating that you must pay before leave can be granted.

howItWorks.title: Each payment creates another
howItWorks.detail: After the leave fee comes a flight, then a medical bill or a customs charge. The requests continue for as long as money keeps arriving.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Lorraine, a retired bus dispatcher, met 'Staff Sergeant Daniel' through a word game app with a chat feature. He said he was a combat engineer on a peacekeeping rotation and a widower with a daughter at boarding school. They moved to a messaging app and wrote daily for seven weeks. Then an email arrived from a 'Leave Processing Unit' with a form: Daniel's emergency leave was approved, but as his named partner she had to pay a $950 replacement fee, in gift cards, so another soldier could cover his post.

The gift cards made her pause. She could not see why an army would want codes from a supermarket rack. She saved Daniel's profile picture and ran it through a reverse image search, which led to the public page of a real serviceman with a different name, along with warnings that his photos were being misused. She stopped replying, kept the messages, reported the profile to the app and told her sister. Lorraine and Daniel are invented for this illustration, but the leave-fee request appears in this scam again and again.

variations.name: The box of valuables
variations.detail: He claims to have been awarded or found cash or gold and ships it to you by 'diplomatic courier'. A fake delivery company then demands clearance fees.

variations.name: Injured in action
variations.detail: A 'military doctor' or comrade writes that he has been wounded and that treatment or evacuation will not begin until you pay a hospital deposit.

variations.name: Retirement or discharge paperwork
variations.detail: He wants to leave the service early to be with you, and says a release fee or a lawyer's charge stands in the way.

variations.name: Receiving money for him
variations.detail: He asks you to accept a transfer or a parcel and pass it on. The funds are stolen from other victims, which turns you into the money mule.

realVsFake.real: Leave is requested by the service member through their own chain of command, at no cost and without input from a partner.
realVsFake.fake: A 'commanding officer' emails you a leave application with a fee to be paid by gift card or wire transfer.

realVsFake.real: US military staff use official email addresses ending in .mil, and other countries' forces use their own government domains.
realVsFake.fake: The 'unit' writes from free webmail, with a rank or the word 'army' squeezed into the username.

realVsFake.real: Serving personnel receive their salary into their own bank accounts and can manage that money online while deployed.
realVsFake.fake: He says his pay is frozen until the mission ends and that only you can cover his costs meanwhile.

realVsFake.real: Deployed troops regularly phone and video call family through ordinary apps when they are off duty.
realVsFake.fake: He says cameras are banned for the whole deployment, yet manages to message you for hours every day.

verify: Save his profile photos and run them through a reverse image search such as Google Lens or TinEye to see whose pictures they really are.
Ask for a live video call today in which he says your name and waves. A real person can manage two minutes; a scammer will have a reason not to.
Search his name and rank together with the word 'scam'. Stolen military identities are often already listed in warnings posted by earlier targets.
Paste two or three sentences from his messages into a search engine, since the same romantic scripts are reused word for word with many people.
Show the conversation to one friend or relative before sending anything. Describing a leave fee aloud to another person usually makes the problem obvious.

payroll-diversion-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: A short, polite email reaches whoever runs payroll: 'I've changed banks and want my salary to go to the new account from this month. What do you need from me?' The name on it belongs to a real colleague, the tone is ordinary, and it lands a few days before the pay run closes, when the inbox is full of routine changes. Nothing about it looks like fraud. It asks for a small administrative favour of the kind payroll staff carry out every week, and it invites a helpful reply.

The sender is not the employee. They found the name and job title on a professional networking site or the company's own team page, then wrote from free webmail or a domain one letter away from yours, with the colleague's name as the display name. Once payroll keys in the new numbers, the next salary goes to an account the criminal controls, often a prepaid card or app-based account opened with stolen identity details. The money is moved on within hours. Nobody notices until the real employee asks why they have not been paid.

The defence is a process rule with no exceptions: bank details never change on the strength of an email. Every request is confirmed by speaking to the employee on the phone number already held in the HR file, or face to face, before anything is edited. A reply to the message does not count, because the reply goes to the criminal. Applied to every change, including those from senior staff and those that arrive on deadline day, that single call defeats the emailed version of this fraud.

howItWorks.title: Staff names are harvested
howItWorks.detail: The fraudster picks an employee from public profiles and identifies who handles payroll, sometimes choosing a senior person because a larger salary is worth more.

howItWorks.title: A lookalike sender writes
howItWorks.detail: The email shows the employee's name, but the underlying address is free webmail or a near-copy of the company domain, sometimes with a different Reply-To.

howItWorks.title: The form is returned
howItWorks.detail: If payroll replies with a change-of-details form, it comes back completed within minutes, sometimes with a forged voided cheque or bank letter attached.

howItWorks.title: The pay run executes
howItWorks.detail: Salary is sent to the new account on the usual date. The payment is genuine and authorised by the employer, so no bank alarm is triggered.

howItWorks.title: Discovery comes on payday
howItWorks.detail: The real employee reports missing wages, often days later. By then the receiving account has been emptied and the employee is still unpaid.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: This is an invented scenario. Ines handles payroll for a plumbing supplies firm with forty staff. Three days before the monthly cut-off she received an email signed by Rob, one of the warehouse supervisors, saying he had moved to a new bank and asking her to update his account 'before this month's run if possible'. The display name read exactly as Rob's always did. She sent the firm's change form, and it came back filled in within ten minutes, with an account at an app-based bank she had not seen him use.

The speed bothered her, because Rob worked on the warehouse floor and rarely answered email before evening. She clicked the sender's name and saw a free webmail address, not the company domain. She walked down to the warehouse and asked him. Rob had not changed banks and had sent nothing. Ines left his details untouched, forwarded the message to the firm's IT contractor, warned the two other people with payroll access, and added a line to the change form stating that all requests are confirmed in person or by phone.

variations.name: Self-service portal takeover
variations.detail: The employee is phished for their HR portal password, and the criminal logs in and edits the bank details directly, with no email to payroll at all.

variations.name: Hijacked real mailbox
variations.detail: The request comes from the employee's genuine account after it was compromised, and a hidden inbox rule deletes payroll's replies before the owner sees them.

variations.name: Fake payroll provider notice
variations.detail: An email styled as your payroll software asks the administrator to 'reconfirm' their login, giving the criminal access to every employee's bank record.

variations.name: Executive pay redirect
variations.detail: The sender poses as a director, counts on staff being reluctant to question them, and asks for the change to be handled quietly and quickly.

realVsFake.real: A genuine employee logs in to the HR portal to change their own bank details, or signs the company form in person.
realVsFake.fake: The sender asks payroll to type the new numbers in for them, and gives a reason why the portal 'isn't working'.

realVsFake.real: Internal email comes from the company's own domain, and pressing Reply shows that same address.
realVsFake.fake: The colleague's name sits over a webmail address or a domain one character off, and Reply goes somewhere else.

realVsFake.real: An employee who has truly switched banks will confirm by phone and can wait a pay cycle if needed.
realVsFake.fake: The sender says they are travelling or in meetings, cannot take calls, and needs it done before the cut-off.

realVsFake.real: A real new account is in the employee's own name, and a payee name check, where your bank offers one, matches.
realVsFake.fake: The account is often a prepaid card or newly opened app account, and the name check returns a mismatch.

verify: Phone the employee on the number already in the HR record, not one from the email signature, and ask whether they requested the change.
Click the sender's display name to reveal the full address, then check it and the Reply-To field character by character against your company domain.
Look in the payroll system's audit log to see whether the employee's bank details were edited through the portal recently, and from which login.
Ask IT to check the employee's mailbox for forwarding or auto-delete rules, which point to a compromised account.
If the pay run has already gone, call your bank's fraud line straight away with the payment reference and ask for a recall request to be raised.

grandparent-phone-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: The phone rings late in the evening or early in the morning. A young voice, crying or short of breath, says 'Grandma? It's me.' Most people answer with a name, and from then on the caller is that grandchild. A cold, a bad line or a 'broken nose from the crash' explains why the voice sounds wrong. Then the story arrives: a car accident, an arrest, a night in a cell. It works because it reaches someone half awake and frightened for a child they love, with no time to think about anything else.

After a minute the 'grandchild' passes the phone to a second voice, a lawyer or police officer who quotes a case number and a bail amount. This person is the one who collects. You are told to withdraw cash and hand it to a courier who will come to the door, to post it overnight inside a magazine, to buy gift cards and read out the codes, or to feed notes into a cryptocurrency machine. A 'gag order' is invented so that you tell nobody. If the first payment goes through, calls about legal fees follow.

One action breaks it: hang up and ring your grandchild on the number you already have, or ring their parent. It takes two minutes, and a real emergency survives a two-minute delay. No court, police force or lawyer collects bail in cash at a front door or accepts gift cards, and none of them forbids a family from talking to each other. A caller who insists you stay on the line and keep it secret is afraid of exactly that phone call.

howItWorks.title: A call at an odd hour
howItWorks.detail: The phone rings when you are likely to be tired or alone. The caller opens with 'It's me' and waits for you to supply a name.

howItWorks.title: The emergency is described
howItWorks.detail: The story involves a crash, an arrest or a hospital, usually far from home, with a reason the usual mobile is unavailable, such as being broken or taken by police.

howItWorks.title: An authority figure takes over
howItWorks.detail: A calm 'lawyer' or 'officer' comes on the line with a case number, explains that bail must be paid today, and warns you not to discuss it.

howItWorks.title: Cash is arranged in secret
howItWorks.detail: You are coached on what to tell the bank teller, often that the withdrawal is for home repairs, then told how the money will be collected.

howItWorks.title: Collection and repeat demands
howItWorks.detail: A courier or rideshare driver takes the envelope. Within hours another call says more is needed for legal fees or the other driver's injuries.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Walter, a retired machinist, was woken at six one morning by a call. A tearful young man said 'Grandpa, it's me, I've messed up,' and Walter answered 'Kyle?' The caller said yes. He had been in a crash in another city, a woman was hurt, and he was at a police station. A man calling himself a public defender then took the phone, gave a case number and said Kyle could be released for 6,500 in cash, which a bonded courier would collect at noon. A judge had barred any discussion of the case.

Walter was at the bank counter with the withdrawal slip when the teller asked what the cash was for. He had been told to say 'a new roof', and saying it aloud felt wrong. He stepped aside and rang Kyle's mobile. Kyle answered from his college library, perfectly well. Walter cancelled the withdrawal, told the teller what had happened, and reported the call to the police non-emergency line. When the 'lawyer' rang back, he let it ring. The people in this account are fictional; the script they follow is a common one.

variations.name: Cloned voice call
variations.detail: A few seconds of audio from a public video is enough for software to imitate a grandchild's voice, so sounding right no longer proves who is calling.

variations.name: Doorstep courier collection
variations.detail: Instead of a transfer, a stranger or an unwitting rideshare driver is sent to your home to pick up a sealed envelope of cash.

variations.name: Hospital abroad
variations.detail: The grandchild is said to be injured while travelling, and a 'doctor' or 'consular official' needs payment before treatment or a flight home.

variations.name: 'New number' text message
variations.detail: A text reads 'Hi Gran, I dropped my phone, this is my new number', followed a day later by a request to pay an urgent bill.

realVsFake.real: A grandchild who is really in trouble can answer a family question and has no objection to you ringing their parents.
realVsFake.fake: The caller dodges personal questions, hands the phone to a 'lawyer', and insists that nobody else is told.

realVsFake.real: Where bail involves money, it is paid at a court or jail, or through a licensed agent, and you receive paperwork for it.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked for cash in an envelope for a courier, gift card codes, or a deposit at a cryptocurrency machine.

realVsFake.real: A police station or law office can be reached through its publicly listed switchboard number, which you can look up yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The 'officer' gives only a direct mobile number and urges you to stay on the line while you go to the bank.

realVsFake.real: Genuine officials do not instruct relatives to mislead bank staff about why they are withdrawing money.
realVsFake.fake: You are given a cover story, such as home repairs or a car purchase, in case the teller asks questions.

verify: Hang up, then ring your grandchild's own mobile number from your contacts. If there is no answer, ring their parent, sibling or partner.
Ask the caller something a stranger could not find online, such as the name of a childhood pet or what you ate together last visit.
If a police station or court is named, look up its main number yourself and call it to ask whether your relative is there.
Agree a family code word today, a single unusual word any relative must say when calling for urgent help with money.
If a courier is already on the way, keep the door shut, do not hand anything over, and phone the police on their non-emergency number.

sources.title: Scammers Use Fake Emergencies To Steal Your Money

zelle-payment-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: It often starts with a text that looks like a bank fraud alert: 'Did you attempt a Zelle payment of $480? Reply YES or NO.' You reply NO, and within a minute the phone rings with your bank's name on the caller ID. The person on the line knows your name, sounds like a call centre agent and says a fraudulent charge is in progress. Because you have just denied a payment, a call from the fraud department is precisely what you expect, and the caller's first job, earning your trust, is already done.

The caller says the way to reverse the charge is to send the same amount to yourself through Zelle. To make that land in their pocket, they first ask you to read out a code your bank has just texted, supposedly to verify your identity. That code lets them enrol your mobile number against their own bank account, or sign in as you. When you then send money 'to your own number', Zelle delivers it to the account that number now points to. It arrives within minutes, and because you sent it yourself, the bank may treat it as a payment you authorised.

The rule is short. No bank stops fraud by having you send money, to yourself or to anyone, and no bank employee needs a code that was texted to you. If a caller asks for either, hang up without explaining and dial the number printed on the back of your card. If a real problem exists, the agent you reach that way can see it. Zelle is built for paying people you know and trust, and a payment you send through it should be treated like handing over cash.

howItWorks.title: A yes-or-no alert text
howItWorks.detail: A message styled as a bank alert asks whether you made a Zelle payment. Replying NO tells the criminal the number is live and that you are worried.

howItWorks.title: The spoofed fraud call
howItWorks.detail: A call follows with the bank's name or real phone number faked on the caller ID. The 'agent' may recite your name and address.

howItWorks.title: A code is requested
howItWorks.detail: You are asked to read back a passcode 'to confirm your identity'. In reality it approves linking your phone number to the scammer's account, or their login to yours.

howItWorks.title: You pay 'yourself'
howItWorks.detail: Guided step by step, you open your banking app and send a Zelle payment to your own mobile number, sometimes in several smaller payments.

howItWorks.title: The money is withdrawn
howItWorks.detail: Funds land in the criminal's account within minutes and are moved out. The caller ends the call or asks for one more 'test' transfer.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Renee, a pharmacy technician, got a text on her break asking whether she had sent a $480 Zelle payment to someone she had never heard of. She replied NO. Her phone rang almost at once, showing her bank's name. A man who introduced himself as being from the fraud department said the payment was still pending and could be reversed if she acted now. He asked her to read out the six-digit code he was sending to verify her, and she did. He then told her to open her app and send $480 to her own mobile number.

She typed in her number, and the confirmation screen showed a recipient name that was not hers. The caller said this was a 'temporary reversal profile'. Renee stopped, hung up and called the number on the back of her debit card. The real agent found no $480 payment and no fraud alert on her account. Because she had read out a code, they reset her online banking password and her Zelle enrolment and added a note to her file. Renee is a fictional character used to illustrate how the call unfolds.

variations.name: 'Business account' upgrade email
variations.detail: A marketplace buyer says their Zelle payment is stuck until your account is 'upgraded', and a forged email tells you to refund an extra amount they supposedly sent.

variations.name: Accidental payment refund
variations.detail: A stranger sends you money from a hijacked account and asks for it back. When the original is reversed as fraud, your refund is gone.

variations.name: Utility shut-off demand
variations.detail: A caller posing as the power or water company says service will be cut within the hour unless an overdue bill is paid by Zelle.

variations.name: Goods that never arrive
variations.detail: Sellers of concert tickets, puppies or rental deposits insist on Zelle, which carries no purchase protection, then vanish once paid.

realVsFake.real: A genuine bank alert asks you to confirm or deny a transaction. If you deny it, the bank blocks it on its side.
realVsFake.fake: Denying the payment brings an immediate call from an 'agent' who needs you to do something in your app.

realVsFake.real: Banks reverse or dispute fraudulent charges internally and never need a customer to move money to make that happen.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says the only way to cancel the charge is to send a matching Zelle payment to yourself.

realVsFake.real: A passcode texted by your bank is for you to enter in the bank's own app or site, and is not meant to be shared.
realVsFake.fake: The caller asks you to read the code aloud 'for verification', which approves their access or enrolment.

realVsFake.real: Zelle shows the recipient's enrolled name before you confirm, so you can see where the money is going.
realVsFake.fake: When an unfamiliar name appears, the caller explains it away as a temporary security or reversal profile.

verify: Hang up and call the number on the back of your card or inside your banking app. Do not use a number from the text or caller.
Open your banking app and look at pending and recent transactions yourself. A charge the caller describes but you cannot see does not exist.
In the app's Zelle settings, check which mobile number and email are enrolled, and tell your bank if your number has been removed or changed.
Before any Zelle payment, read the recipient name on the confirmation screen. If it is not the person you mean to pay, cancel.
If you read out a code or sent money, phone your bank's fraud line now, say it was a scam, and ask them to secure online banking.

google-voice-verification-code-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: You have posted an advert, perhaps for a sofa, a room to rent or a missing cat, with your mobile number on it. A reply comes quickly from someone keen. Before going further they say they have been caught out by fake listings and want to check you are a real person, so they are sending a six-digit code to your phone and would like you to read it back. The request sounds like ordinary caution, the code arrives from Google as promised, and reading out six numbers seems to cost nothing.

The text was not sent by the buyer. It was sent by Google, because the scammer is partway through setting up a Google Voice number and has entered your mobile as the phone to link it to. Google checks that the person signing up controls that phone by texting a code to it. If you pass the code on, the scammer completes the setup and holds a working US phone number that is tied to yours. They use it to place adverts and call other victims while hiding their own identity.

The rule is that a code texted to your phone is typed only by you, into the service that sent it, for something you started. Nobody proves they are human by reading a code to a stranger, and no marketplace asks buyers and sellers to verify each other this way. The Google message itself says not to share the code. The moment anyone you met through an advert asks for one, the conversation is over, however reasonable the explanation sounds.

howItWorks.title: Your number is collected
howItWorks.detail: The scammer finds your mobile number on a listing, a lost pet poster or a dating profile, or asks for it so they can 'text instead'.

howItWorks.title: A Voice signup begins
howItWorks.detail: On their own device they start creating a Google Voice number and enter your mobile as the linked phone that Google must verify.

howItWorks.title: Google texts you a code
howItWorks.detail: A real message from Google arrives with a six-digit verification code and a line telling you not to share it with anyone.

howItWorks.title: The code is handed over
howItWorks.detail: Told it proves you are genuine, you read the digits back. The scammer types them in and the new Voice number is activated.

howItWorks.title: Your number fronts their fraud
howItWorks.detail: They go quiet or block you, then use the Voice number in other scams. Your own mobile is now recorded as the phone behind it.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Mateo, a graduate student, listed his road bike on a local marketplace with his mobile number in the description. Within twenty minutes someone called 'Karen' messaged to say she would pay the asking price and collect that evening. She added that she had lost money to a fake seller the week before, so she used a 'verification service' to be safe. A text would arrive with a code, and he only needed to send her the six digits. The message came through seconds later.

He had the code half typed when he read the whole text: it began 'Your Google Voice verification code is' and ended with a warning not to share it. He had never used Google Voice, and a code from Google had no connection to selling a bike. He told Karen he would not send it. She replied twice more, insisting it was standard, then stopped. Mateo reported her profile to the marketplace and removed his phone number from the listing. This scenario is made up, but the exchange follows the usual script closely.

variations.name: Lost pet poster call
variations.detail: Someone rings the number on your missing pet notice, says they have found the animal, and wants a code to confirm you are the true owner.

variations.name: Rental or roommate enquiry
variations.detail: A would-be tenant or landlord asks for the code before arranging a viewing, claiming they need to screen out fake adverts.

variations.name: Dating match 'safety check'
variations.detail: A new match says they verify everyone they meet and asks you to read back a code before swapping numbers or arranging a date.

variations.name: Codes for other accounts
variations.detail: The same excuse is used to obtain a WhatsApp registration code or an email password-reset code, which hands over that account directly.

realVsFake.real: Google sends a Voice verification code only to confirm that whoever is signing up controls the phone it was texted to.
realVsFake.fake: The stranger describes it as their own security check and says the code proves you are not a bot.

realVsFake.real: Marketplaces verify members inside their own apps and never ask one user to collect a code from another.
realVsFake.fake: The buyer says a past bad experience means they personally need a code from you before meeting.

realVsFake.real: A genuine buyer asks about the item's condition, the price and when they can collect it.
realVsFake.fake: The questions skip the item entirely and move straight to your phone number and the code on its way.

realVsFake.real: Someone who really wants proof that you exist can ring you, or simply meet in a public place.
realVsFake.fake: A phone call or meeting is refused, and only the six digits will do, as fast as possible.

verify: Read the whole text before doing anything. It names the service that sent it, and the Google Voice message says not to share the code.
Tell the buyer you will not send any code but are happy to speak by phone. A genuine buyer carries on; a scammer argues or disappears.
If you already shared the code, open Google Voice, sign in with your own Google account and try to add your mobile as a linked number.
If Google warns that the number is in use on another account, choose the option to reclaim it, which removes it from the scammer's.
Report the profile through the marketplace's report button and remove your phone number from the public listing, using in-app messages from now on.

canada-post-text-scam.author: Scam or Safe editorial team
intro: A text arrives headed 'Canada Post' saying a parcel is being held because of an unpaid fee of $1.45 or an incomplete address, with a link to sort it out before the item is returned. So many people are waiting on an online order at any given time that the message meets someone expecting a delivery almost wherever it lands. The amount is small enough to pay without thinking, and the page behind the link carries the red branding and a tracking bar that make it look like routine admin.

The fee is a pretext. The form asks for your name, address, date of birth and phone number, then your card number, expiry date and security code. Many versions then show a screen asking for the one-time code your bank has just texted. That code is not approving a $1.45 charge. It is typically approving your card being added to a mobile wallet on the criminal's phone, or a much larger purchase. The personal details are kept too, and may be used later by a caller posing as your bank's fraud team.

The rule that settles it: track parcels only by typing the tracking number from your order confirmation into the Canada Post app or website yourself. Canada Post says it does not text or email about a delivery unless notifications were requested for that item, and when a delivery is missed the carrier leaves a paper Delivery Notice Card telling you where to collect it. A surprise text asking for a payment through a link can be deleted without checking anything further.

howItWorks.title: A parcel-on-hold text
howItWorks.detail: The message uses the Canada Post name and says an item cannot be delivered because of a small unpaid fee or a missing address detail.

howItWorks.title: Reply to unlock the link
howItWorks.detail: Some versions tell you to reply Y and reopen the message. iPhones disable links in messages from unknown senders, and replying switches the link on.

howItWorks.title: A cloned tracking page
howItWorks.detail: The link opens a page in Canada Post colours with a made-up tracking status and a 'schedule redelivery' button leading to a form for your personal details.

howItWorks.title: Card details for a tiny fee
howItWorks.detail: You are asked for card number, expiry and security code to pay a dollar or two. The fee itself may never be charged at all.

howItWorks.title: The bank code is captured
howItWorks.detail: A final screen requests the passcode from your bank. Entering it can approve the criminal adding your card to the wallet on their own phone.

caseStudy.title: An illustrative example
body: Amrit, who works in a university admissions office, was waiting for a pair of boots he had ordered online when a text arrived: 'CANADA POST: Your parcel is on hold due to an unpaid fee of $1.45. Update your details here.' The page looked right, with a red header and a tracking bar stuck at 'Delivery attempted'. He entered his address and his credit card details. A new screen then asked for the verification code his bank had just sent 'to confirm the payment'.

He opened the bank's text to copy the code and read the line above it: the code was to add his card to a mobile wallet on a new device. That had no connection to a delivery fee. He closed the page without entering it, called the number on the back of his card and had the card cancelled and reissued. The retailer's own order page showed his boots were with a different courier altogether. He forwarded the text to 7726. Amrit's story is illustrative and not a real case, but each step matches how these texts operate.

variations.name: Customs or duty demand
variations.detail: The text claims import duty is owing on an international parcel and asks for card payment through the link before the item can be released.

variations.name: Incomplete address hold
variations.detail: No fee is mentioned at first. You are asked to 'confirm' your street address, and a small redelivery charge appears on the next page.

variations.name: Email with a tracking button
variations.detail: An email in Canada Post colours shows a fake tracking number and a 'Track your item' button that leads to the same card form.

variations.name: Follow-up bank call
variations.detail: Days after you fill in the form, someone phones as your bank's fraud team, quoting the details you entered, and asks for more codes.

realVsFake.real: Canada Post says it only texts or emails about an item when notifications were requested for that delivery.
realVsFake.fake: The text arrives out of nowhere, from an ordinary mobile number or an email address, about a parcel it never identifies.

realVsFake.real: After a missed delivery, the carrier leaves a paper Delivery Notice Card naming the post office where the item is waiting.
realVsFake.fake: The message says the parcel will be sent back unless a redelivery fee is paid online within a day.

realVsFake.real: Duty and tax owing on an international parcel are tied to a real tracking number and can be paid when you collect the item.
realVsFake.fake: A tiny fee is invented with no tracking number attached, because the aim is your card details, not the money.

realVsFake.real: Genuine tracking happens on Canada Post's own website or app, reached by typing the address or opening the app yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The link uses a lookalike address with extra words or an unfamiliar ending, and the page disappears within days.

verify: Find the tracking number in your retailer's confirmation email and enter it in the Canada Post app or on the website you typed yourself.
Check the retailer's order page to see which courier is actually carrying your parcel. It is often not Canada Post at all.
Look at who sent the text. A random mobile number with an overseas prefix, or an email address, is a sign the notice did not come from a postal service.
Forward the message to 7726, the spam reporting number used by Canadian mobile carriers, then block the sender and delete the thread.
If you entered card details, call the number on the back of the card now and ask whether it was added to any mobile wallet.
